speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: MR. SHARP    REFERENCE TO QUESTION BY MEMBER FOR QU'APPELLE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday in this house the hon. member for Qu'Appelle directed a question to the Prime Minister and asked whether any minister of the government had held discussions with either the management of Maclean's magazine or any of the editorial staff with regard to Liberal policy and the editorial policy of Maclean's magazine. You, Mr. Speaker, said this was a very interesting question but far too long for immediate answer. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle then said:
Mr. Speaker, then I would like to direct my question to one of the ministers, if I may. Have I your permission, sir?
You replied:
I have suggested to the hon. member that the question be put on the order paper because it requires a very detailed answer.
Today, when I returned to my office, I found that my office had been approached by Mr. Victor Mackie of the Winnipeg Free Press who said that in an interview with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle I had been named as the minister to whom he had meant to direct his question.
My question of privilege is this, that the hon. member should put his question on the order paper where it can be answered adequately, rather than spreading rumours and gossip through the press.
High! Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition): The hon. member for Qu'Appelle is absent and all I have to say, Mr. Speaker, is that the statement made by the minister is a gratuitous one and has no basis in privilege.

On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, would the Secretary of State for External Affairs bring the house up to date on the perilous situation in southeast Asia? Would he advise what representations, if any, Canada has made to the United States in connection with this matter and whether, in the circumstances of the last few hours, he is able to give the house a more optimistic view than he could give yesterday?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since the Prime Minister and I informed the house yesterday of the situation as we saw it, there have been no fresh military developments in the crisis in Indochina. As the house knows, there was a meeting yesterday of the security council, and that meeting has been adjourned sine die to permit private negotiations to take place.
Since yesterday the main interest has centred around the probable reaction of the Chinese people's republic. In an official statement the Peking government has in effect reaffirmed and strengthened an earlier stand indicating that China would take action in the event that hostilities in Indochina were extended to North Viet Nam. This statement however, is ambiguous and there is no clear indication what kind of action is contemplated.
The Soviet union has predictably criticized the United States but again has not indicated what specific action if any it proposes to take. An examination of the statement of the Soviet ambassador at yesterday's security council meeting does not offer an indication of what action the Soviet union has in mind,

Inquiries of the Ministry other than to make a general condemnation on the part of his government of the action taken by the United States. They have failed to realize that the action taken by the United States was, as the Prime Minister said yesterday, obviously one of a defensive character in pursuance of the right of a country to defend itself against an attack wantonly made against some of its ships. The British government has likewise taken a stand in support of the right of the United States to defend itself against unprovoked attacks on ships operating on the high seas.
This morning I received a protest from the North Vietnamese foreign minister, as have other countries I suspect, with regard to other alleged incidents, but not with regard to the attacks on the United States destroyers which were made, presumably, pursuant to the authority of the government of North Viet Nam.
It will be noted that yesterday Mr. Adlai Stevenson, on behalf of the United States, took no objection to the suggestion that, as the United States has put forward its appreciation of the situation, North Viet Nam should not be denied the right to be called before the security council at some future time to give reasons for the action it took, or to respond to the position taken by Mr. Stevenson on behalf of the United States. I do not believe anything could usefully be added at this moment.

The minister mentioned that the security council adjourned to permit private negotiations to take place. What is the significance of that? Does he mean private negotiations under the aegis of the United Nations, or outside the United Nations?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Canadian ambassador to the United Nations has been in touch with the ambassador of the United States and with representatives of other countries. I do not believe that at this time I could add anything more regarding the character of these negotiations.

May I address a supplementary question to the Prime Minister. Does the Canadian government intend to make any representations or take any steps designed to prevent an escalation of the hostilities in southeast Asia? Is the Canadian government offering in any way to conciliate between the disputants in the hope of preventing this explosive situation from becoming worse?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister);
speechtext: We have already been in touch with the United States government on this matter, as I said yesterday, and expressed the strong hope that no action would be taken which would result in what the hon. member calls the escalation of the incident. As I said yesterday, we expressed the hope that any retaliatory action required in defence will be limited to the necessities of the circumstances. I do not know what useful steps we can take with regard to the conciliation of the two governments concerned, since we have no representative in North Viet Nam. But we are members of the international commission in Viet Nam, and perhaps our membership there will give us an opportunity in the days ahead. If so, we shall not hesitate to take advantage of it.

In that connection, has there been any communication by Canada with the other two members of the commission as to any beneficial course which might be taken at this time; because action now is certainly most important in this connection? Canada's recent stand regarding the reconvening of this commission appeals to some of us to have been quite unjustified.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I do not know
what the right hon. gentleman means when he speaks of Canada's attitude toward the reconvening of this commission. The international control commission in South Viet Nam is in operation, and I may say that our representative on that commission has been in touch with the representatives of Poland, and India, the other members of the commission, with regard to this matter. I suspect that what the right hon. gentleman meant was the calling of the 14 power conference.
That is what I had in mind.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The calling of that conference, as I have indicated on a number of occasions, does not in our judgment necessarily offer the solution to this problem. The North Vietnamese have violated the agreements that were entered into in Geneva in 1954 and 1962. If the communists would observe those agreements there might be none of the present difficulties in Viet Nam or, for that matter, in Laos.
However, I have indicated that, if it is thought desirable that there should be such a conference, we would of course participate. But in arriving at our point of view, we have had to bear in mind not only our own

view of what was desirable, but as well the view of other countries. In this instance, bearing in mind the heavy responsibility of the United States, our action has not been unrelated to what we believe to be its position.

The United Kingdom is fully aware, of course, of all the circumstances to which the hon. gentleman has alluded, and with its vast experience in international affairs the United Kingdom must have had sound reason for its application. Why is it, therefore, under the circumstances, that Canada chooses to drag its feet, as it were, in this connection?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Canada, of course, is not dragging its feet in this matter. There is no difference between the positions of Canada, the United Kingdom and the United States in this matter. My right hon. friend is likely referring to the statement attributed to the British foreign secretary last Saturday, when he made a suggestion that the members of the international control commission in Laos should call a conference of the three factions in Laos itself. In answer to that, I pointed out that the commission had no authority to call such a conference.
But I may say, as I did indicate the other day, we were very active in consultations with the properly constituted government of Laos to see that steps were taken so the three factions could meet. As a result of those representations, and representations made by India as well, the prime minister of Laos, Souvanna Phouma, is taking steps to bring together the three factions in Laos to discuss not the calling of a full 14 power conference, but the terms and conditions under which such a conference would meet.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. May I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs this question. If, as he says, the North Vietnamese have violated the agreements of 1954 and 1962, would it not seem to be the responsibility of Canada, along with the other two members of the commission, to report to the 14 nations who set up the commission that their task has been made impossible, and ask for a meeting of the 14 nations in order to receive fresh instructions? Why is Canada not taking some action, rather than allowing the situation to drift along and deteriorate from day to day?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Canada has certainly taken action. As we have indicated several times within the course of this parliamentary session, Canada has pointed
Inquiries of the Ministry out that because of the refusal of the representative of Poland to act on the basis of a majority decision in the commission, it was not possible for the commission to follow courses which we felt were in the interests of the situation both in Viet Nam and in Laos.
With regard to the commission reporting to the conference as a whole, that is not the procedure laid down in the Geneva accord. The commission reports to the co-chairmen, who are the United Kingdom and the Soviet union. Canada and other countries, recognizing that the procedure and the machinery for settlement exists in the Geneva accord of 1954 and 1962, is not, if this can be avoided, anxious to afford to communist China the opportunity of using a larger forum simply for the purpose of making propaganda.
This is a consideration which has to be borne in mind. However, we have taken the position that if all members who attended the meeting in Geneva in 1962 and in 1954 believe there is no other course now open but to have a conference, Canada will be anxious to do its part.
All members?
All members.

Mr. Speaker, as an Anglican I wish to address a question to the Minister of Justice on behalf of one of the other bodies of opinion in Canada. In view of the fact that the Canadian Bill of Rights guarantees the right of the individual to equality before the law and the protection of the law and freedom of religion and freedom of speech, and in view of the fact that any petition to parliament must contain a prayer, would the minister inform the house how persons of the Rationalist

society or others who do not believe in any form of prayer can present a petition to the House of Commons?

maintopic: USE OF WORD "PRAYER" IN PRESENTING PETITIONS
speechtext: Order. This gives me the opportunity to make a short statement. It seems to me this question is completely out of order. In the first place, the hon. member is asking for a legal opinion, which he should not do at this time. Second, it is not within the jurisdiction of the government to decide this question, in that the form of petitions has been prescribed by parliament and not by the government. Third, the premise of his question is wrong, for under present day usage the word "prayer", to my way of thinking, has no particular religious significance but is rather a traditional form of usage and is in fact used as a form of courtesy. For these reasons, therefor, I must rule that the question is out of order.

Interim Supply

speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek rises on a point of order.

speechtext:

Mr. Chairman, is it proper to continually interrupt those who have the floor because their remarks seem to irk some Conservative members of this house? I have quoted the exact wording of the commission's report. If this afternoon, I am making a point of reading into the record some paragraphs of that report, it is precisely because I think the time has come for people to open their eyes and for Quebec farmers to realize in what way the agricultural assistance policy favours western farmers in comparison with the assistance offered eastern farmers. The same can be said of ARDA policy.
In the west, grants are given, but in the province of Quebec, loans are authorized. People are pushed into debts and thus, a solution is supposed to have been found.
In a letter to the farmer the question is asked:
Who may borrow?
Are any persons aged 21 or over eligible for an ordinary loan, whose main business is or will be agriculture on an economic unit-
Reference is made to an economic unit, but we know very well that according to the federal government policy, family farms in the province of Quebec are considered as uneconomic units and we know that 75 per cent of Quebec farms are marginal income farms on which a family could not make a decent living under the present conditions of market and support prices.
This means that within the present federal farm policy, it is impossible to borrow under the farm loan legislation. Nothing can succeed in the province of Quebec under the federal government's way of thinking.
Maclean's magazine recently published a report of several pages on the Quebec farmer's position. It was quite clearly stated that the Quebec family seemed very attached and rooted to its farm, where those people wanted to live decently under the federal farm loan legislation, but that it is impossible for the Quebec farmers to obtain the amounts which are available to companies or large operations in the prairies under the standards established by the federal Farm Credit Corporation. In Quebec there is no such possibility, unless the formula of consolidating farms is accepted or collective farms are established, as they exist in other areas.
That is why it would be logical to call that legislation the "rural displacement act". On 20220-409
Interim Supply
the other hand, as mentioned by the representative of the Catholic farmers' union, the farmers do not so much want credit or loans as support prices or the guarantee of a reasonable profit on their products. The farmer wants an income that will make it possible for him to live decently; what he wants is not just loans, credit and debts, but markets.
I mentioned yesterday that, when one hears about federal farm policy, one gets the impression that there are only wheat producers in Canada. No mention is made of our eastern farmers, whose production depends to a very large extent on the production of feed grain.
Ever since we came here we have been urging the federal government to consider the advisability of building, at suitable locations along the St. Lawrence river, elevators from which feed grain could be supplied to eastern producers at reasonable cost, so they could offer their respective products at competitive prices. For instance, take poultry and eggs. In eastern Canada, we could specialize in this field, but none of those suggestions seems to have been taken seriously.
In view of those facts, Mr. Chairman, I think the Quebec farmer is beginning to realize that he must not count on the federal government for any assistance. That is why they turn more and more to the government of the state of Quebec. And we should not be surprised if their representations are finally expressed in a manner quite contrary to our wishes, we who sit here, namely a Canada united from coast to coast.
In the field of federal policy, under cooperative federalism, practically the same results are obtained as previously, and I wonder if Quebec farmers will not be justified in asking in turn what others have requested, namely independence, because it will be easier for them to have access to a government which would understand them, while here some rural areas get everything they want, thanks to their majority.
I realize that the problems of the eastern farmers are not those of the western farmers and that efforts must be made to solve the problems of eastern producers, but it is not through loans that the question will be settled, even if the possibility of a loan up to $100,000 was admitted, as long as it will be felt that Quebec marginal farms cannot be eligible to federal loans it will be a policy of nothingness, a wait-and-see policy; but pending hopelessness, I wonder if Quebec farmers would

Interim Supply
not be justified in turning elsewhere than to Ottawa tor an opportunity to solve their problems.
We have problems in the field of markets. Commissions have been set up to assure the exportations of wheat through the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) by guaranteeing the payment of wheat sales to foreign countries. Was anything done to find markets for some feed grain surpluses? Not much. There are statistics to prove that. Through the Canadian wheat board, feed grain sales are controlled by very powerful trusts which, in turn, control the sale of feed grain and shorts, which makes it possible to control the purchase of cattle through packers. It is the same interests from one end to the other which control and have in hand the fate of agriculture in eastern Canada.
There is for instance the field of hog production. It costs the Quebec farmer $6.19 more than the western farmer to feed a hog. How is it possible to be competitive on this market unless there are subsidies from the federal government to guarantee to the eastern producer a reasonable price for his production. With support prices, I am convinced that he would become an expert in his field, because we already have organized farms in the province of Quebec where certain private enterprise has invested huge sums of money.
I remember that ten years ago already, during an election campaign, much was made about eggs coming from Poland. That is an obvious contradiction with regard to the warranted aspirations of egg producers in eastern Canada who were asking for price stabilization in that field.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.
However, I must tell him that I took into account the points of order which interrupted his speech earlier this afternoon.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak today I trust that none of those people who are in favour of changing the national flag will accuse me of filibustering the flag debate. I have let it be known in some quarters that I am in favour of the retention of our present distinctive national flag.
Hear, hear.

In speaking today I am following the cue of the hon. member for Algoma East, the leader of the Liberal party, who when in opposition in December of 1962- and I sat across the aisle with him-spoke on

the then motion for interim supply. The member said in part:
Mr. Chairman, this discussion on interim supply has roamed far and wide. Indeed, I have taken part in the roaming myself and I make no apology for that. If I speak again, it is to deal with a specific matter arising out of the request for interim supply. But I think it should be pointed out that, while the discussion of this matter has roamed far and wide, some very important matters have been brought before the house which could not have been brought before the house in any other way at this time...
We have had to take advantage of this kind of motion in order to bring these matters to the attention of the house in the hope that government spokesmen would deal with them in replying...
It is a traditional and fundamental right of parliament to vote taxes before they are collected and to approve expenditures before they are made. When these rights are ignored, when they are violated, parliament Itself is being violated and we are taking a step toward its destruction. No matter how wide a circulation we give and no matter in what form.. .and no matter how much we may talk about Magna Carta.. .no matter how emotionally we may wrap ourselves up in parliamentary or national flags, both these rights I have mentioned are being deliberately and systematically violated by the present government...
Now, Mr. Chairman, we are being asked to vote blind on another monthly instalment of the annual expenditures.. .Then we are being asked to go home...and come back to issue another blank cheque... As I have already stated, parliament's examination of, and control over, government spending is the very foundation of our democratic parliamentary system...The government will not be explaining.. .its plans... It will be reporting to the house on old history, on what it has already spent...Mr. Chairman, the Canadian people are entitled to something better than perpetual interim supply.
In this motion before the house we are being asked to vote interim supply for the fifth and sixth months of the present fiscal year, and with very, very little discussion of any of the major departments and major expenditures. I intend to devote my attention today to the expenditures of the C.B.C. and the B.B.G., as they are familiarly known. I have done a little bit of research into this matter during the past two weeks, and I am not at all happy with my findings with regard to parliamentary control or investigation of the expenditures of the C.B.C. Here we are being asked to vote the fifth and sixth months of interim supply for C.B.C. expenditures, which in the book of estimates that we all have for the fiscal year in which we are now operating amount to a total of $88 million, which is something over $7 million a month. This interim supply vote will give the C.B.C. better than $14 million, with very little discussion with regard to their operation.

I checked with regard to the C.B.C. expenditures for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1964, and I had the assistance of very able civil servants. I would report to this committee that the only discussion which occurred in this parliament on the estimates of the C.B.C. for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1964 took place on December 21, 1963, when nine months of that fiscal year had already passed and only three months remained. This discussion took place after the supper hour on the evening of December 21, and you can imagine, Mr. Chairman, the thorough going over the C.B.C. estimates had at that time on December 21, the night the house adjourned for the Christmas recess.
With regard to the fiscal year ending March 31, 1963, the C.B.C. estimates were never discussed in the House of Commons. Following the election in April, 1963 this government tidied up the matter and we okayed the expenditures in July, 1963, long after the expenditures concerned had been made.
The C.B.C. estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1962 were never discussed in this house. They were passed on September 22, 1961, as will be seen from pages 8757 and 8758 of Hansard. The total expenditure forecast, and which was passed on that day, September 22, 1961, was $70,418,000. I should like to quote the words of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate on September 22, 1961 with regard to those C.B.C. estimates. As reported at page 8757 he said:
I am not going to oppose the carrying of the vote right now...there are two considerations in the minds of the opposition in agreeing to the carrying of this vote...The second reason is that the session has already been so prolonged. But we do hope that in taking this position... we will not read in half the newspapers in the country tomorrow that, notwithstanding the shocking increase in the cost of the C.B.C., parliament dealt with the item in 10 minutes.
As I say, $70 million worth of estimates were passed on that day, September 22, 1961.
The estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1961 were discussed at some length on July 8, July 12 and July 13, 1960 and totalled $62 million. The estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1960 were discussed on July 18, 1959, only and passed that same day. I have gone back to show, Mr. Chairman, the amount of attention which has been paid the C.B.C. estimates in this House of Commons during the past five years, and I have to say that the entire matter is being allowed to get out of hand.
Yesterday afternoon the public accounts committee of this house tabled its fifth report
20220-409J
Interim Supply
with regard to questions it had asked the chairman of the C.B.C. in regard to the operation of the C.B.C. during the years 1962 and 1963. This was a request by the House of Commons. I have in my hand a copy of that report, which is a report by members from all parties in the house. Paragraph 7 is as follows:
The committee expressed concern over the increasing cost of the corporation's annual operating requirements which the president stated he believes will continue to increase in size each year in future-
Then the committee points out:
The president indicated that the estimates for Montreal and Toronto, shown on the corporation's balance sheet at March 31, 1963 to have been $83 million, have since been further revised and are expected to cost $105 million. The committee would also record that it has since noted from the corporation's balance sheet as at March 31, 1964, tabled by the Secretary of State in the house on July 14, 1964 that the present estimates of the future cost of consolidation of facilities for the corporation is stated to be $128 million.
In the name of the taxpayers of Canada let me ask this committee, how far are we going to allow this crown corporation to roam without some check being placed on its operations?
Hear, hear.

Then paragraph 7 continues:
The committee expressed grave concern over the size of these large capital outlays estimated by the corporation to be required to provide for the consolidation of facilities, as opposed to the extension of services to areas not now adequately served...
Nevertheless, the committee is seriously concerned at the levels the corporation's spending on operating and capital account have reached since television was first introduced into the national service in 1955.
Let me emphasize, Mr. Chairman, that I am speaking in this committee of supply on interim supply; I am not filibustering the flag resolution: The paragraph continues:
The committee emphasizes that the House of Commons, through the committee of supply, has a definite responsibility to exercise control on the extent to which public funds should be expended for the maintenance and development of the national broadcasting service.
This report is drawing the attention of the House of Commons as a whole to the ever increasing expenditures of the C.B.C. I point out that in 1962, according to the Auditor General's statement which the public accounts committee was investigating, the C.B.C.'s total operations cost $78 million. In 1963 they amounted to $81 million; and according to the blue book for the present fiscal

Interim Supply
year the operating expenses will amount to $88 million if there is no cut-back of any kind.
What is the fate, Mr. Chairman, of questions asked by a mere member of parliament as to how the C.B.C. is conducting its affairs or what it is doing? These questions could not be shushed off more abruptly if they were asking about the internal operations of the Bank of England, which is no concern of ours. We are simply asking questions with regard to the operations of the C.B.C., and to show the sort of interesting answer, if not informative, which is given. I would like to refer the committee to Hansard for July 29, 1964. As reported at page 6116 the hon. member for Dorchester asked:
What fees were paid by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation during 1963 to (a) Andre Lau-rendeau (b) Jean-Louis Gagnon (c) Jacques Hebert (d) Jean Marchand (e) Mrs. Jeanne Sauve-
Whoever she is. The answer comes back from the Secretary of State:
I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that it is not customary to require the corporation to disclose the fees paid to program participants because of the competitive business in which the C.B.C. is engaged.
I would ask, why is the Canadian government engaged in competitive business? Why are the funds of this nation pitted against taxpaying commercial interests in the community who are printing magazines and newspapers, putting up billboard advertising, engaging in direct mail advertising, private station advertising, and who have to compete with a national competitor who is able to draw on the taxes of this nation?
The hon. member for Vancouver East asked a question on March 9 of this year with regard to a promoter of perversion, Mr. Gins-burg from New York, who had appeared on the C.B.C. The hon. member asked how much the C.B.C. paid Mr. Ginsburg for his contribution to the "culture" of this country, and the following is part of the answer given by the parliamentary secretary to the Secretary of State, as reported at page 673 of Hansard:
It is considered to be not in the public interest to require the corporation to give such information as it could affect the corporation in the competitive business in which it is engaged.
Once more I ask, why is the Canadian government engaged in competitive business against taxpaying commercial enterprises in this country?
On March 23, 1964, I myself asked this question, as found on page 1329 of Hansard:

What has been the advertising revenue, month by month, secured by radio station CJBC, Toronto, since it became an independent station, separate from a network?
Back comes the echo from the Secretary of State:
It has not been customary to require the corporation to give information which could adversely affect it in the competitive business in which it is engaged.
Why in the name of God is it in a competitive business? On July 15, 1964 the hon. member for Port Arthur asked the following question, as found on page 5495 of Hansard:
1. What was the chronology, with an explanation for each step, in the C.B.C.'s dealings with the production by R. Kelly entitled "The Good Life" from its genesis to the decision not to present it to television audiences?
Hon. members will recall the question. Back comes the echo, this time from the parliamentary secretary:
The C.B.C. is engaged in a competitive business and has customarily been left free to conduct its day to day business without being obliged to make public details of its production operations.
This thing is getting absolutely impossible to put up with. I have in front of me here three different statements. I do not like to use the word "criticize" but that is the only word I can use. I will not say "comment", which is a little milder. I do not like criticizing public servants or civil servants since they cannot answer in the same forum I am using but, believe me, when civil servants make the statements they do in what has come to be known in the broadcasting industry as the troika report, the memorandum on broadcasting issued by Alphonse Ouimet, president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, in 1964, and the comments they make in the annual report of the C.B.C. and in speaking to the association of Canadian advertisers in Toronto, they are asking for a reply and this is the place where they should get it, because they come here looking for supply, usually on an interim basis. I should like to read from page 9 on the memorandum on broadcasting which I have in my hand and which is available to all members of the house. Mr. Alphonse Ouimet proclaims as follows:
The C.B.C. was created three decades ago as the publicly owned national agency.
At the top of page 14 in the same memorandum he also states:
The corporation was established as an instrument of national purpose.
If there ever were mouthfilling words or phrases signifying next to nothing, it is these

two statements. Many members are kind enough to say that I do not show my years, but that is because of the good attention my wife gives me. I am 62 years of age, and I can stand here today and state that I was present at the meeting held in Ottawa under the aegis of the then prime minister, R. B. Bennett, when the decision was made as to who should be appointed the first general manager of the C.B.C.
When Mr. Ouimet says the C.B.C. was created three decades ago as a publicly owned national agency and that the corporation was established as an instrument of national purpose, I should like to give him the facts of life. At that time the radio world was in a state of flux, in that not as much was known about radio then as today, and Canada was being assigned six channels by the international control commission. Of course there were hundreds of businessmen seeking those channels. They saw this new medium of communication as a sure-fire profit maker. The government of the day and the commentators of the day-I mean those of the newspapers and magazines-maintained that the airways were the property of the public, and that since they were limited and Canada was being offered six channels, to put them into private hands was the same as giving a man a licence to print money.
If you want me to be specific, the meetings in Ottawa were held in the Chateau Laurier hotel and the east block of the parliament buildings. They lasted for a good number of days. We dealt with the applications which had been received for the position of general manager. I was connected with an organization then, as I was for almost 40 years, that was operating the first radio station to be operated in Canada. I am frequently asked by-I will use the word-young punks in the C.B.C. what gives me the right to talk about radio or television. They were not born when I first became interested in the radio world, and I have been greatly interested in it ever since.
Where is the Secretary of State?

The C.B.C. was not established as an instrument of national purpose. It was established so the government could maintain control of these channels, and there was no intention at that time of engaging in competitive business. I tell you quite frankly that in those days we did not have the briefcases that lawyers carry around today. We used gladstone bags and we used to pick them up
Interim Supply
and travel from here to there carrying our gladstones.
The committee of selection, of which I was a member, recommended a certain appointment and Mr. Bennett said, "If that is your choice he will be appointed". We recommended as general manager a gentleman who had been operating with the British Broadcasting Corporation in the British Isles. The reason he was recommended was that the British Broadcasting Corporation at that time did not accept advertising of any kind in competition with the established advertising media. We figured that if he was appointed general manager of the Canadian organization he would fully understand the system, the government would be advised that the British system was the best, and we would have a radio system that would not be competing with the established commercial advertising world.
Over the years changes have come about, and today we have a publicly owned system competing actively with a privately owned organization with both of them seeking advertising moneys. I believe that in this day and age the C.B.C. is unnecessary in this country. It is not performing a single function that cannot be performed just as ably and just as well by the private organizations that now exist in this nation.
And a little cheaper.

Yes, and I would say better as well. In only half an hour I cannot express all my feelings or the feelings of the advertising world with regard to the C.B.C. I am glad this is only interim supply we are considering, because we will have another opportunity to discuss the C.B.C. when the main estimates come forward. I want to quote a statement that appears in Dennis Braithwaite's column in the Globe and Mail of June 12 in which he is dealing with the C.B.C. and uses these words:
The C.B.C. does not know what it is there for any more. Its only purpose seems to be to go on existing. It is rapidly reaching the point where it will soon be impossible for any outside investigator to trace the source of a C.B.C. decision, which is presumably the bureaucratic ideal.
Believe me, I could not agree more than I agree with Dennis Braithwaite's comment in the statement I have just read. These are very expensively prepared reports, the memorandum on broadcasting, the statement of Alphonse Ouimet, the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, and the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation for 1963-64. The statement that

Interim Supply
Mr. Ouimet made before the association of Canadian advertisers is very nicely printed. Many people take these statements as the most authoritative word that can be said on such a vast subject. On page 5 of the annual report of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation we find this statement, and I want hon. members to pay close attention to it because it is really something:
The directors epitomize a basic tenet to the effect that broadcasting exists to serve people, and not vice-versa.
My God, for $70 million we find that broadcasting exists to serve people and not people to serve broadcasting. On page 8 of what is known in the advertising world as the troika report, which was prepared by Messrs. Jamieson, Stewart and Ouimet, we find this really shocking announcement:
We believe the principle of hearing all cases in public is sound.
You know, until I read that I had a lot of doubt in my mind with regard to whether we were being fair to applicants for television and radio licences by making them appear in public. When I read that Messrs. Ouimet, Stewart and Jamieson put in this report to the government "We believe the principle of hearing all cases in public is sound", I thought of Moses coming down from the mountain top. I have a note here which reads "I wonder if Mr. Ouimet endorses the ten commandments", but that is outside the point.
On page 28 of this memorandum we read:
A second principle recognizes the needs of the national service as predominant.
Now, is this a personal statement by the chairman of the C.B.C. or did it come down from mount Sinai? I cannot tell. It is called a principle.
A second principle recognizes the needs of the national service as predominant.
Well, for Pete's sake, you do not know how far you can go in this ridiculous situation.
Now, on pages 19 and 20 of this memorandum on broadcasting you will find a statement by the chairman to this effect:
For the past 30 years the number of public inquiries into broadcasting have been more than adequate. The great lack has been the absence of a planned program of assessment and review...
A major public examination of the over-all Canadian broadcasting system and its components at regular intervals of ten years is suggested for consideration.
The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation could be operated under a public "charter" or mandate for a period of years which would coincide with the intervals between major public studies. This mandate would state generally the aims, objectives and

scope of the corporation and include a firm basis for corporation financing for the ten year period.
When I read that the C.B.C. wanted a ten year charter, as they call it, I was really dismayed. The people who pay taxes in this country have to work every day in order to earn the wherewithal with which to keep the C.B.C. operating on its present gargantuan scale. Then I began to think of the disciple who came to the Lord and asked Him how to pray. In the eleventh chapter of Luke you will read how one of the disciples said "Lord, teach us to pray". Then we read:
And He said unto them, when ye pray, say... give us day by day our daily bread.
Now, Mr. Ouimet cannot take the time to ask for his sustenance on an annual basis. Parliament has to meet on an annual basis to pass the army bill, but it should not have to meet on an annual basis for the C.B.C.; once every ten years should be enough.
That is a pretty good reference.

I have a better one. In the sixteenth chapter of Exodus you will read that the children of Israel were murmuring against the Lord because of hunger. I quote:
Then said the Lord unto Moses, Behold, I will rain bread from heaven for you; and the people shall go out and gather a certain rate every day, that I may prove them, whether they will walk in my law or no.
And it shall come to pass, that on the sixth day they shall prepare that which they bring in; and it shall be twice as much as they gather daily.
And Moses and Aaron said unto all the children of Israel, at even, then ye shall know that the Lord hath brought you out from the land of Egypt... At even ye shall eat flesh, and in the morning ye shall be filled with bread; and ye shall know that I am the Lord your God...
And the children of Israel did eat manna 40 years, until they came to a land inhabited; they did eat manna, until they came unto the borders of the land of Canaan.
If the C.B.C. board of governors had been running that operation they would only got food four times in ten year instalments and would not have had to worry about daily bread. These people believed that if they got bread daily they were very fortunate and blessed amongst the people of the earth; that is the way the Lord treated it because the C.B.C. board of governors had not been created yet to evolve this system of ten year instalments.
What perplexes me immensely is the use of this word "mandate". The C.B.C. are everlastingly telling us they operate under a mandate, they operate under a parliamentary mandate. I have in my hand a copy of the

annual report, and on the very first page you will read this:
Parliament has accepted these stated aims and objectives which are now known as the parliamentary mandate-
This is written by the C.B.C. board.
Parliament has accepted these stated aims and objectives which are now known as the parliamentary mandate-
I ask you to look at pages 6 and 7 of the memorandum on broadcasting which was issued at the same time. You have the flatfooted statement there that parliament has accepted these stated aims known as the parliamentary mandate. On pages 6 and 7 of the memorandum on broadcasting the chairman of the board writes:
For many years the corporation has made reference to its parliamentary mandate, a term which is sometimes misunderstood.
Then there is this statement:
In the corporation's view, and in my personal view, the acceptance by parliament of the C.B.C. role as developed by its trustees-
Note that phrase.
-as developed by its trustees constitutes a parliamentary mandate which is as effectively binding as though it were spelled out in detailed legislation.
He admits there is no detailed legislation spelling out the parliamentary mandate, yet he talks about it incessantly, incessantly and incessantly. There is no parliamentary mandate. This C.B.C. is not a thing apart from the taxpayers of Canada, nor from this parliament of which we are members. It is a crown corporation, and it should be held responsible to this parliament of ours, and should be held responsible on an annual basis.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I have to bring to the attention of the hon. member the fact that his time has expired.
No, no.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. We have to have the unanimous consent of the committee.
Agreed.

I wish to thank the committee for their indulgence. I regret that I have not contributed much to this interim supply debate, but I will do my best. Yesterday I purchased on Sparks street at Smith's book store the August edition of Show. It is a monthly magazine and contains an article headed "The Ten Year Decline of TV", by Harriet Van Horne. This book costs one dollar and it is well worth five. The writer,
Interim Supply
Harriet Van Home, is a woman who is decrying the disappearance of live shows from television and radio. It is all canned today by tape, and the actors and actresses do not make the money they used to make. This is the burden of her story.
There are some excerpts here I should like to read into the record with regard to the future of television. I believe the future of television is a matter that comes within the purview of a motion for supply when they are asking for as much as $15 million in interim supply for the C.B.C. I should like to read the first couple of paragraphs:
The current-which is to say banal, cheap and joyless-state of television recalls a story Charlie Weaver, the Mt. Idy philosopher, used to tell on the old "Tonight" show. Its hero was Charlie's cousin, who enjoyed a spectacular rise in show business.
"He started small with a hand organ and a monkey," related Charlie. "And today he's got a pipe organ and a gorilla."
As the article says:
There you have a capsule history of television. From merry little comedies and honest, moving drama to "Million Dollar Movie" and "Bonanza" in living colour-with real blood. From engaging little parlour games with no grand prizes to rigged quiz shows involving millions.
She writes on in much the same way. An interesting thing about television's future is that we are told it is worth $128 million in Montreal and Toronto alone, not to mention what they want to spread around the rest of the country. Here is another comment from the same article:
Today there is almost a sense of embarrassment about t.v. watching. It has become a secret vice, like marijuana or stag reels.
We are talking about when television probably began to decline, and this phrase is in here:
On the other side of the set, people date the decline of t.v. from the day they moved the set to the bedroom. Or the day it broke and they forgot to get it fixed for a month.
To me that is a capsule history of the popularity of t.v. and radio today. You have the $64,000 rigged questions, something which was proven in the courts. You have the Nielsen ratings showing how many people were looking at programs they did not even know existed.
There is another case here I thought I should draw to your attention showing the way people in this business are not entirely held above suspicion. This writer in the American magazine says:
In some large cities, such as Austin, Texas, a shrewd business mind and an obliging friend or

Interim Supply
two on the FCC, have maintained monopolies. Viewers who do not wish to see what the only channel is offering can go read a book (though in Texas, one suspects, it's not often done).
The final conclusion in the article is:
Some observers say that more people may be watching, but they're in the under 12 or the shut-in group. Or they're the unemployed, or the group that has no consumer power to speak of, beyond the essential food and clothing funds supplied by public welfare.
The day will come, say those who have lost faith in t.v.'s potential, when sponsors discover that they cannot sell their products via television. The people who can afford to buy won't be watching.
I now would like to swing over to another angle of the t.v.-radio business that should be drawn to your attention. This week's issue of Newsweek, now on the stands, has a long article about pay t.v. in California. The issue of Time magazine which came out yesterday also has an article on pay t.v. in California. In yesterday morning's Montreal Gazette Dink Carroll-I knew him when he played in the backfield for McGill University in the early twenties-had a long column dealing with the moneys being paid to football teams, baseball teams and hockey teams for television rights, and it is quite interesting to read because Dink makes the statement:
Harold Ballard, one of the principal stockholders in the Toronto Maple Leafs, revealed that the club sells its television rights for Saturday night games for $500,000 a year.
"Our present contract expires in two years," he added. "When it's up for renewal our asking price will be $2,000,000 a year and that figure could change rapidly. We may even ask $5,000,000."
Those big baseball and football television contracts have got everybody talking that way.
Then Dink goes on to say:
This isn't the hockey season, but N.H.L. club owners operate on the theory that making a dollar is never out of season.
I draw this to the attention of the committee for this reason. Dink Carroll points out that the owners of the teams are interested in the television money, but I ask what about the players? Do the owners not think they are interested in that television money? I can tell you at this date, August 6, that a brief will be submitted to the Fowler commission on radio and television on behalf of professional athletes, which will demand some compensation for the entertainment they are giving the public on Saturday nights, Saturday afternoons, and Sundays. At present the owners of these professional clubs treat the players as little more than trained seals.
If you follow the rules in football you know the teams can only ask for a certain

number of times out, but if you check television practice you find there are three or four times as many times out as are allowed, in order to let the commercial be shown on the television broadcast. How many of you know that three minutes before every professional game ends in Canada there is a time out so that the advertiser sponsoring the broadcast can get in his final clincher?
I was told by a professional hockey player you all know, but who shall be nameless in this chamber, "You haven't any idea how often they change the puck in the national hockey league." I do not know whether they need better pucks or more uninterrupted viewing, but it is just a little insight on this television business. Jim Proudfoot of the Toronto Star had a column in last Saturday's paper dealing in part with television. I asked some west coast members if they knew about this particular matter and they said they were not aware of the situation. Jim Proudfoot says:
Lions are beaming their home games into a Nanaimo theatre. With the Victoria outlet, this gives them 4,000 closed circuit seats.
I say to you that with the ferment the radio and television world is in today, it is no time to be giving anybody a blank cheque for 10 years, let alone for one year; and I oppose the suggestion for a ten year-what shall I say-solitude or respite from the prying eyes of members of the House of Commons. When they talk about a 10 year respite I would point out that on page 11 of the annual report of the C.B.C. there appear these words of the chairman:
The number of variables involved means that there are constant changes in the planning lists from year to year and sometimes oftener.
Now, standing on that great principle, because you do not have to read very far until that statement is called a statement of principle, they say, "Give us our largesse in ten year instalments so we won't have to come to you hat in hand and ask for money every year." They must be prophets of the first water to be able to make statements like that.
I am in favour of selling the assets of the C.B.C. to tax paying commercial interests, and when they have made such a sale we will get an income from the private stations such as we get now in a limited way from the existing stations. I say to the government, get out of the competitive business of the advertising world.
Spoken like a good Tory.

I am a good Liberal. I have not sunk that low yet.
On page 10 of the address by the president of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation to the association of Canadian advertisers there is this statement:
We believe the C.B.C. is the most influential advertising medium in this country.
This is a great big mouth-filling expression, and on page 46 of the memorandum on broadcasting we have Mr. Ouimet again extolling the tremendous advertising value of the C.B.C. saying:
As I stated earlier C.B.C. is the only truly national advertising outlet available to Canadian business.
When I hear that this is the greatest advertising force in Canada today, I cannot figure how Eaton's ever developed to their present position. They did not have the benefit of any radio advertising; they did not have the benefit of any television advertising. We have to admire the Hudson's Bay Company for reaching its present prosperous state. This company, too, grew and expanded without the benefit of radio and television. The C.P.R., likewise, was built up in an era when there was no radio or television advertising. How they were able to get ahead before the C.B.C. came into existence I have not yet been able to figure out.
It is a known fact in the advertising world that the C.B.C. sets its rates, not according to cost but according to how much it can get. I was talking this over the other day with an hon. member of this house, but before I tell you what he said, Mr. Chairman, let me read some more from Mr. Ouimet. This is Mr. Ouimet speaking:
The private sector has a proper concern with the total advertising picture but it is perhaps unfortunate that from time to time the commercial activity of C.B.C. is believed responsible for a drop in revenue in certain parts of the private sector.
Here is the great prophet himself speaking:
This feeling is not supported by the facts. The total of Canadian net advertising revenues in 1963 was over $594 million. Of this amount, non-broadcasting media accounted for approximately $467,300,000, private broadcasters for $103,800,000 and the C.B.C. for $23 million.	'
And the member to whom I was speaking said to me "That is a very limited bit of the total advertising, being only 3 per cent." I said, "You never were in the advertising business, my friend. It only took a small hole in the bottom of the Titanic to sink her to the bottom of the Atlantic and it only took a small gash in the Andrea Doria to send her to the bottom of the sea, and when you have a com-20220-410
Interim Supply
petitor in the advertising world who is subsidized by the taxpayers' money, he sets his rates according to what he can get, not according to cost of production." It is a known fact that the C.B.C. is paying 80 per cent of the cost of these sports spectaculars. The sponsor gets full credit for promoting them, and the big fellows in the advertising world cannot afford to stay off the C.B.C., they get their advertising so cheaply. So when a commercial enterpriser approaches representatives of these companies and says: I should like you to use my billboards, or order some pamphlets, because I have a printing press, or take some newspaper space or magazine space, or take some time on my radio or television station, the big fellow says "No, I can use the C.B.C. so much cheaper than I can use you." I say that what is going on is not fair to the commercial advertising world and that the C.B.C. has got to get out of the commercial advertising business.
But Mr. Ouimet says, as will be found on page 43:
A retreat from advertising dollars by the C.B.C. on the grounds that it would help the over-all private sector would not be warranted.
I have written on the side: "Who says so?" I can get a thousand men to subscribe to my statement without the slightest trouble in the commercial world of Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg and Vancouver, if further support is needed for what I am saying.
The committee has suffered these remarks in patience and silence. I have exceeded the time allotted to me. Let me sum up by saying that I do not believe the C.B.C. should be in existence. I do not believe it should have any commercial advertising business whatever. Since we shall have another opportunity of discussing the C.B.C. when the next interim supply resolution comes up for consideration, or when the general estimates are before us, I will withhold some further comments I have to make on the subject. Let me say I am not counting on the general estimates of the C.B.C. to come before us soon, because I have read the five year history-[DOT] how nobody ever discusses the affairs of the C.B.C. And when we make inquiries, we are told: "This is a competitive business and we don't tell nothing to nobody."
What did the public accounts committee have to say? In its report yesterday, the last paragraph reads:
The committee recommends that the Secretary of State table an official memorandum in the house presenting the corporation's views and its replies to each of the matters dealt with by the royal

Interim Supply
commission in its report No. 19, and that this be done before the estimates of the corporation are considered by the house.
This recommendation was made because Mr. Ouimet, giving evidence before the committee, explained that the Glassco royal commission had apparently failed to understand the nature of the problems of broadcasting. Well, I thank whatever gods there be for Mr. Alphonse Ouimet, who is able to point out that the commission did not understand the nature of the problem. Now, on the basis of this recommendation, the C.B.C. will be able to take the next six, seven or eight months preparing the corporation's views, and its replies to each of the matters dealt with by the Glassco commission.
I say: Stop all capital expenditure by the C.B.C. until we get a little fact into this fantasy which is now running around the country and until we can discuss the operations of the corporation intelligently and in detail, without being told "Keep quiet, because it is engaged in a competitive business".

I am sure the committee has listened with attention to the views expressed by the hon. gentleman. While he was speaking I have been viewing the front benches of the government. Their reaction to what he said, and the views he expressed, would lead me to believe that his popularity among them will not be tremendously increased.
I wish you could have seen them, Mr. Chairman. There is the Solicitor General. He had a lugubrious appearance during the progress of the hon. gentleman's remarks which one would expect him to have if he were reviewing a capital sentence. The attitude of the Minister of Justice was: There is certainly no justice in this. The Minister of Finance-

I would ask him, while I am on my feet, to restrict or limit his remarks to the resolution now before the committee.
Mr. Chairman, my question of privilege is this-
Mr. Chairman, I ask you to exercise your authority in regard to this interruption that goes on from time to time by this hon. gentleman.

Mr. Chairman, I was referring to the various ministers-

Mr. Chairman, the interruptions of the hon. gentleman from Lapointe are so frequent whenever one is discussing the government that the completeness of his alliance must from time to time bring heartburn to the Minister without Portfolio, who dealt with both that hon. gentleman and the hon. member for Villeneuve so effectively in the last election.
Hear, hear.

I was about to mention the fact that the Secretary of State, as the 20220-410J
Interim Supply
custodian of culture and as the minister responsible for the C.B.C., while he was in the house earlier today did not see fit to be here during the progress of the speech of the hon. gentleman. I look back over the years, as far as the C.B.C. is concerned, and see Right Hon. R. B. Bennett bringing before parliament the measure for the establishment of this body as a national institution-and so it must remain. I would not want anybody to conclude that, while in reference to expenditures what the hon. gentleman has said will receive somewhat general support, we in this party have changed our view in regard to this institution. We stand where we have always stood, namely on behalf of a national corporation for radio and television, in order to represent and epitomize the best things of our nation.
Having said that, I want to add this. In the last few weeks and months there has been on the part of the C.B.C., in the examination of so-called freedom of speech by so-called independent commentators, a tendency to bring parliament into disrepute and use virulent language to criticize members of parliament or the official opposition as such. This was very obvious in a broadcast this morning. I am not going to spoil the record of parliament by giving the name, but only this morning there was a contemptible exhibition by a so-called commentator in which a personal attack was made, which by no stretch of the imagination could be dictated by other than excessive uncontrolled and virulent partisanship. I want to make that very clear.
I believe in freedom of speech; but one thing the C.B.C. will have to guard against, if it is to maintain its reputation for being completely neutral, is the degree to which in recent months-and I am emphasizing that again-the commentators have been using that forum for the purpose, not of giving a picture of parliament but to indulge in statements bordering on libel and slander. I said a moment ago that we support, and shall continue to support, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and the objectives that were set forth in the act passed by parliament. We do believe, however, that there is no justification whatever for the failure of this government to bring the C.B.C. before parliament and a parliamentary committee for the fullest investigation and examination. We have the right to information.

Hear, hear.

We have an example in British Columbia-I realized that in raising this matter it might not bring me any favour with some of those in high places in the C.B.C.-in connection with the Kitsilano property out there, when there is widespread demand on the part of the people of Vancouver that a portion of the Kitsilano property should not be turned over to the C.B.C., whether absolutely or for a period of 35 years. Yet the head of the C.B.C., when speaking out there, indicated that it is only a question of when it will be taken over by the C.B.C., regardless of the wishes of the people of British Columbia. That is not in keeping with the responsibility that rests on the president of the C.B.C.
Mention has been made of the pyramiding costs of the C.B.C. As far as advertising is concerned, one or two commissions have dealt with that matter. Advertising was limited in the recommendations of those commissions. I feel sure this is something the Fowler commission will have to give earnest attention to, so that above everything else private advertising will not find itself unfairly competed against by a public enterprise which from year to year is requiring ever increasing amounts.
We believe in the necessity for and the responsibility of parliament to exercise control over public funds that go to the C.B.C., which now reach massive amounts. We believe-and we have not been able to make any advance in this connection-that a committee of the house should have placed before it the C.B.C. picture, to the end that after the fullest examination recommendations may be made by the people's representatives regarding the rightness of the expenditures being made, so that a proper control of such expenditures may be ensured: because, after all, this is the taxpayers' money. Have we been able to get it? Nothing of the sort. It has been brushed off, as the hon. member said, by supercilious answers of almost contemptuous import-"This is a matter you have no right to look into. You must not ask this question. The C.B.C., in the public interest, says it shall not be answered". Only yesterday, as was mentioned a moment ago, the public accounts committee made certain recommendations in this regard. When we were in office we decided that in order to make the public accounts committee effective it should have a member of the Liberal party, the then opposition, as chairman. That tradition is now being followed by the present government and this committee has been an effective one.

This committee pointed out yesterday in its fifth report that as of March 19, 1963 the cost of the Montreal and Toronto facilities of the C.B.C. had been $83 million. However, the president of the C.B.C. advised the committee last month that this figure had been increased to $105 million. Since that time the corporation in its annual report for 1963-64 boosted its estimate of the future cost of consolidation of facilities in the two cities to $128 million.
I ask, Mr. Chairman, where are we going? Are we going to permit the creation by parliament of a corporation that can spend without any conception of control on the part of parliament? This is a matter which a committee of parliament could look into. Finally, the committee emphasized that-
-the House of Commons, through the committee of supply, has a definite responsibility to exercise control on the extent to which public funds should be expended for the maintenance and development of the national broadcasting service.
I rise, Mr. Chairman, simply to say that parliament today has little or no control over the degree to which the C.B.C. expands or spends money, money which is to a very large extent the taxpayers' money. We have the right to have that control. There is no way in which we can get this committee unless members of parliament are given the freedom to vote in this regard regardless of party. We are being denied this, and it is something that we are entitled to and to which the Canadian people are entitled. I support to the full the basic principles which Mr. Bennett enunciated and which are incorporated in the legislation of the 1930's regarding independence for and the integrity of the C.B.C.; but such does not demand a freedom from the fullest examination, and such should not permit the granting of that independence 10 years in advance without examination by parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is not my intention or purpose to delay the passage of interim supply, which I am sure all members of the committee would wish to see disposed of at the earliest possible moment, but in view of the absence of the Secretary of State I should like on behalf of the government, to say a word or two in reply to some of the criticisms-in fact, I do not think it is going too far to say attacks-which have been made on the C.B.C. this afternoon.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: By whom?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Name your own member.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: What do you want to do, canonize him?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not mind mentioning names if necessary but that is not my purpose and I do not want to get into that kind of debate.
In the opinion of the Liberal party and of some other parties in this house the importance of public broadcasting in Canada can hardly be exaggerated. As a member of the government and as a member of the Liberal party I want to make it perfectly clear that we believe in public broadcasting. We believe in the C.B.C. and we intend to support that institution.
While I am on my feet I should also like to deplore the personal attacks which have been made on the president of the C.B.C., Mr. Alphonse Ouimet, who I suggest is a dedicated public servant of whom all Canadians can properly be proud.

speakeroldname: Mr. Muir (Cape Breton North and Victoria):
speechtext: Is he above criticism?
Get on your feet.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I was asking whether the president of the C.B.C. is above criticism, like the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not intend to get into that kind of discussion, Mr. Chairman. What I am saying is that when a public servant like Mr. Ouimet is attacked in the house I believe that some member of the government should get up and support him, and that is what I am doing now. That is something that I would do on behalf of any public servant who was singled out in this way.

Would the minister permit a question. He has just made the statement that he would protect any public servant who had been charged in this way. Would he not tell the house who made these charges against Mr. Ouimet, and what the charges were?
