speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I was referring to the committee that has been set up under the chairmanship of Mr. Robert Fowler and which was announced by the Secretary of State some time ago. If any hon. members have questions on that score perhaps they would ask them of the Secretary of State tomorrow.

Mr. Chairman, I very much regret having to take up any time of the committee, but certain events have taken place in the last couple of weeks, indeed in the last 24 hours. As there will be no other opportunity in the foreseeable future to get an answer to these questions, I am afraid I will have to take six or seven minutes of the committee's time to request the government to give some sort of answer now. I direct my request to the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs and ask them to give an explanation of what certainly appears to be a two-faced, fence-sitting, wishy-washy foreign policy in southeast Asia.
In the first instance, I refer to the government's position in the current Indonesian and Malaysian question. On the one hand, apparently we are going to provide increased economic and military assistance to our friendly

Interim Supply
sister nation in the commonwealth, Malaysia, whose territory is under constant, unprovoked attack by Indonesia. Dr. Sukarno, the Indonesian dictator, has already sworn to destroy Malaysia. On the other hand, we apparently are giving increased economic and perhaps even indirect military assistance to Indonesia. It is well known that the economy of that country is in a shocking state of disorganization due to the neglect and mismanagement of Dr. Sukarno. Yet this government is endeavouring to help keep him in power and is giving him at least moral encouragement in his unprovoked aggressions against peaceful and friendly states by continuing to give him hundreds of thousands of dollars every year of Canadian taxpayers' money.
Just what does this largesse consist of and how much does it amount to? We do not know. All we can get from the Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs are evasive and contradictory answers. For example, at the recent meeting of the committee on external affairs on Thursday, July 16, the Secretary of State for External Affairs was a witness, and as found on page 1598 of the proceedings the hon. member for Brandon-Souris asked this question:
Did I understand the minister to say that Canada is providing assistance to Indonesia?
Yes.
Of what kind?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It is mostly teaching but some equipment and some food.
I then refer to the meeting of the committee on external affairs on Tuesday, July 21 last. The witness before the committee on that occasion was Mr. Moran who is in charge of the external aid branch. As found on page 1629 the hon. member for Brandon-Souris asked these questions and received these answers:
How is the $850,000 for other commonwealth countries allocated? This is the information which I understood was going to he forthcoming.
I can give that to you. Burma. $350,000; Indonesia, $350,000; Viet Nam, $150,000.
Are these not commonwealth countries?

Those are non-commonwealth countries.
Note the figure there, $350,000. In the house on Wednesday, July 29 last I put a question to the Prime Minister. As found on page 6120 of Hansard I asked the following question:
A supplementary question. I was wondering if the Prime Minister can tell the house whether
CMr. Nesbitt.]
the government is planning to continue aid to Indonesia in view of these arrangements with Malaysia.
I was referring to a question asked by the hon. member for Three Rivers about aid to Malaysia.

Mr. Speaker, the only economic aid to Indonesia at present is in the form of flour or wheat to the extent of some $400,000, I am informed. This matter was mentioned to the prime minister of Malaysia, and he understood the position. There is no intention to interfere with that shipment, but we will not be sending to Indonesia any defence equipment or strategic material of any kind.
It is all right for the Prime Minister to say that the prime minister of Malaysia understood the situation. What else could the poor man do when he came here to ask for gratuitous aid? Hon. members will note that Mr. Moran told the external affairs committee on one occasion that $350,000 worth of wheat was being sent to Indonesia. The Prime Minister told us the amount was $400,000, and in the committee on external affairs the Secretary of State for External Affairs told us that aid to Indonesia was "mostly teaching and equipment but some food".
The only implication anybody can draw from these statements is that there must be vast amounts of money being spent on teaching and equipment if $350,000 or $400,000- no one seems to know which figure is right- is being spent on food for Indonesia.
I refer now to a document which was submitted to the members of the committee on external affairs, and which I presume is available to anybody, by the external aid branch. The document lists the aid to various countries, and on page 6 Indonesia is dealt with and we get a different story. We find there these words:
Since 1950, funds totalling $3,988,000 have been made available by Canada to Indonesia for development purposes. A large part of this amount has been in the form of wheat flour valued at $1,875,000, including $325,000 worth of flour in 1962-63.
Among the 73 Indonesian trainees studying in Canada in 1962-63, the largest groups included undergraduate students in science and engineering and in medicine. Others included students of public administration and earth sciences.
Here is the interesting part:
Two Canadian advisers served in Indonesia in 1962-63. A Canadian flying instructor continued his assignment at the Indonesian air academy-
Apparently the other is a statistician. What we are doing supplying a flying instructor presumably to the Indonesian air force I do not know. It may be said that perhaps he is simply teaching civilian flying, but I have no doubt in my mind that this flying instruc-

tor is helping to train the Indonesian air force and in this way we are certainly giving indirect military assistance to a small degree, to say the least, to Indonesia.
Under the circumstances I think that the house and the Canadian people are entitled to an explanation of what can only be called the two-faced behaviour of the government and also a complete, specific and detailed explanation of just what assistance is being given to Dr. Sukarno. All we have been receiving so far are contradictory and evasive answers.
The second instance to which I wish to refer is the position of the government with respect to the present crisis in Viet Nam. The statements of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, both in reply to questions in the house and in statements to the press and on television outside the house, are only capable of one interpretation, namely that the government does not approve of the actions of the United States government in the North Viet Nam area. Of course, this is exactly the interpretation that the press has taken with regard to this matter. To be fair I will say that today the observations of the Secretary of State for External Affairs did seem to have a little backbone in them in this regard, but not too much.
As far as we know, and the facts do not seem to be too much in dispute, P.T. boats from bases in North Viet Nam attacked units of the United States seventh fleet about 65 miles off the coast in international waters. The attackers were driven off but next day the attack was renewed.
In spite of this unprovoked aggression on the high seas, which was also clearly an act of war, and notwithstanding what can only be described as a very delicate and sensitive situation, the United States government replied in the only way the communist aggressors could understand, namely destroy the bases from which these attacks were being launched. Now, it seems the United Kingdom, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs told us this afternoon, and the allies of the United States in western Europe with the possible exception of France, approved the action of the United States. However, apparently the approval of this government is not so pronounced in this instance. The government should make it quite clear that it places itself firmly behind the United States. It should not, by any vague statement or by silence, give assistance or comfort or perhaps even tacit approval to the communist aggressors in southeast Asia.
Interim Supply
President Johnson has made it quite clear his country will not spread the war and will only reply to warlike attacks in kind for the purpose of preventing further attacks on United States forces in international waters. All of us in Canada are proud of the various mediation efforts in which Canada has successfully engaged since 1945 under successive governments. All of us wish Canada to continue this role in international affairs. This does not mean we should adopt a lofty posture of detached interest or, worse still, tacit approval of illegal acts of war on the high seas, particularly when our closest friends and allies are those attacked.

Mr. Chairman, the speech by the hon. member for York-Humber has resulted or will result in about four other speeches this afternoon. The Leader of the Opposition made a speech, followed by the Minister of Finance, and I shall speak for a few minutes. I believe the hon. member for Medicine Hat may speak as well. There are two things I like about the hon. member for York-Humber. He speaks in a very entertaining way and the house is very much alive when he is speaking. In addition, he is very frank and very honest. He does not believe in the principle of public broadcasting and he says so quite frankly. This is in contrast to many people in the country who really do not believe in the principle but hesitate to make a frontal attack.
I was very interested when the hon. member for York-Humber said that the government should sell the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. This remark was greeted with a great deal of approval from the Conservative benches. I believe it is quite significant, however, that the Leader of the Opposition got up later and made a point of saying he believed in the principle of public broadcasting, despite what some of his backbenchers may have indicated by their desk pounding.
When it suits members of parliament, they quote the views of various organizations in this country which have taken certain positions. Today this suits my purpose. I am going to remind hon. members that the Canadian federation of agriculture, the Canadian labour congress and the Canadian home and school association as well as other bodies have supported the idea of public broadcasting in Canada. I suspect this is the reason that all cabinets, of whatever party, have continued to support the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. This was why the hon. member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings, when he was minister of national revenue, fought off his

Interim Supply
own members continually. Cabinet ministers realize the widespread support there is in the country tor public broadcasting, substantially as it is at the present time. They will allow the C.B.C. to be used as a whipping boy regularly, as the hon. member did this afternoon, but no substantial attack can be made upon it to reduce its effectiveness in the country.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I think you can well accept the principle of public broadcasting of radio and television, and within that principle make certain criticisms of the operations of the corporation and perhaps of the board of broadcast governors. It may be that the C.B.C. spends too much on administrative expenses and not enough on programs. This may be, although I suggest we have not had any real investigation to And out whether or not that is so. It may be that they spend too much capital on buildings, at points, but I suggest that we really will not know that unless we can make comparisons with similar organizations in other countries.
Some horror has been expressed at the fact the C.B.C. has asked for a charter for a period of ten years. I think this is a rather long time, and I do not believe they should have a charter for that period of time. I do agree however that they should receive a charter for a certain number of years, perhaps three or four. The Leader of the Opposition expressed great horror at this lack of parliamentary control. Quite frequently he refers to the mother of parliaments at Westminster as a model for us to follow. I would suggest the same is true of the British Broadcasting Corporation. I believe there should be a periodic review by parliament of the spending and plans of the CB.C., but I do not believe this should be on an annual basis. I feel there are practical reasons for this. Every time the C.B.C. is called before the house, we have a real witch hunt. I do not think they can do a very effective job if they have to face that situation annually. While I do not agree with a ten year charter, I think some lesser period should be recommended for an investigating committee.
A great deal of horror was expressed by the hon. member for York-Humber about increasing budgets. I should like to know about some public body in this country which does not have an increasing budget, whether it is a city council, a schoolboard or whatever it may be. The country is growing and we have more people. In order to service more people, we have to spend more money. Private corporation budgets are growing as well.

Some hon. members expressed great horror that $88 million may be used for the C.B.C.'s budget. Nobody has objected to the fact that over ten years this country has spent approximately $15 billion for defence that may be of very doubtful value. I mentioned this in an earlier debate.
There is just one point upon which I think I could agree with the hon. member for York-Humber, Mr. Chairman. He did not like the idea of the C.B.C. being in the advertising field. I do not like it very much, either. I believe that in so far as television is concerned we have to accept it because the costs of television products are very great. If the C.B.C. did not receive certain revenues from advertising for television productions, they would come here and ask for more. Then there would be more complaints because they were asking for more money. I believe there is one side to it where they can operate without commercial revenues. I am thinking of the radio network. It seems to me that with all the wavelengths we have available in this country there ought to be at least one in every major centre of the country to which you could tune and not have to listen to advertisements. I recognize they are absolutely essential to commercial broadcasting. This is one of the reasons they exist; they cannot pay their way any other way. However, in so far as the C.B.C. radio network is concerned, I suggest we could well get along without commercials.
This procedure would have two beneficial effects. It would please the listeners who want that kind of broadcasting and the advertisers could go to the commercial stations. This would increase their revenues.

I am only going to take about three minutes this afternoon. There are some very interesting points raised in some of the speeches regarding the C.B.C. It is obvious from the response that was given to some of these speeches that there is a widespread support in this House of Commons for an examination into the C.B.C. by a committee of this house, notwithstanding the fact that the Fowler commission has been set up outside of the house.
Now, Mr. Chairman, this has been adequately proven by the remarks made previously this afternoon. There has not been a thorough examination of the C.B.C. spending program for the last five years. As has been pointed out, the vote for the last fiscal year 1963-64, went through after supper on December 21, the date for prorogation of that particular session.

The Minister of Finance also said this afternoon that it is obvious to him all hon. members of the House of Commons agree that the house should in fact have some control over the expenditures of the C.B.C. Surely, if there has been no examination in detail for the last five years, we are not in fact effectively exercising that control which it is our responsibility to exercise. Only a few minutes were spent during the last fiscal year on expenditures of something like $78 million. The year before that they were not examined at all, and the year previous they were introduced and passed the same day. In fact the Minister of Finance made a good argument for the setting up of a committee of the house to inquire into these expenditures.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond supported that when he stated there has not been a recent investigation of the allocation of funds by the board of directors of the C.B.C., but he went on to say it should not be done annually, that these examinations should have a longer interval between them If there had been an examination of C.B.C. expenditures at any time during the last four or five years, if there had been an opportunity for hon. members to make an examination in depth and find out where the policy is set, and get some reasons from officers of the C.B.C. for the policies they have pursued, there would not have been built up that animosity which exists at present on the part of hon. members toward the operations of the C.B.C.
Nothing would be more beneficial than to bring the opinions of hon. members and of the executive of the C.B.C. into harmony, and to make a fair study of the C.B.C. expenditures and bring them out into the light of day. I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the Minister of Finance and the Secretary of State,-and I notice the latter two are not present,-to give an undertaking, after the demonstration they have seen in this chamber this afternoon, to set up a committee of the house to go into this problem that is frustrating and bothering many hon. members. When the light of day is thrown on these activities I believe there can be a little harmony between the house and the C.B.C.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the resolution carry?
Carried.

Before the resolution carries I would like to put forward for the third time-and I am told the third time is lucky- my request, in accordance with the suggestions made yesterday and today, that the
Interim Supply
resolution now before the committee for two months' interim supply be withdrawn and there be substituted for it a resolution for three months' interim supply.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is this agreed?
Agreed.

Before this is agreed to, I would like to say a few words. We have had the resolution on interim supply before us for some time now, and I have not taken any time to speak on it. We are presently being asked to honour a commitment that was made in a negotiation on something which was originally suggested by the leader of the New Democratic party. I think that the government and the official opposition, particularly the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition, have been making a farce out of parliament in the last few days.
It seems to me we are being asked to provide another month's supply when we are not going to have any recess. Asking for three been done, and in asking for three months' only two departments have been passed, and half the year has gone, is really stretching it, unless the government is willing to make some concession to members of parliament themselves.
If arrangements which were studied by a committee of the house had been put into effect we might have found that the financial portion of the government's business, including the estimates, would have been completed in the early part of the session, as they are in other parliaments. This has not been done, and in asking for three months' supply it means it will be late in the fall before we come to discuss those departments that have not been opened, and those that have been opened but have not been completed. Unless we are given a better timetable than this, I suggest the government is abusing the authority it has in asking for the extension of supply.
If we are not smart enough as members of parliament to be able to sit down and arrange the business of parliament so that it meets the needs of the day and the needs of the country, then 1 think we are going to have to act in a dog eat dog fashion, and have the true personalities of the Prime Minister and the Leader of the Opposition clash. We all know that when the Prime Minister went away for several days the Acting Prime Minister was able to accomplish a greater amount of business than had been accomplished for a considerable length of time, leaving only four items of business to be completed before

Interim Supply
a recess, items which still remain with us after many weeks. To be fair about it I should also mention that when the Leader of the Opposition was away for several days the same type of co-operation was arranged.
We have a personality clash that is affecting every member of parliament, and it is about time we made some arrangement concerning what we are to do about this particular clash. When we see the way the very legitimate and well planned approach to a compromise, initiated by the leader of the N.D.P., has been treated, we must realize that every member of the house is being abused and every elector in the country is being abused.
I would like to know whether the Leader of the Opposition really wants an election. I would like to know whether the Prime Minister wants an election? In every vote the house has taken the government has had a fairly substantial majority, and so long as it continues to give us legislation and leadership it will continue to have that support. But now the government is failing to do that. If the Leader of the Opposition wants an election he should say so. At present we are in an impasse because the government cannot govern and the opposition is not putting forth its proposals. All we are faced with is this personality clash that is causing such a great deal of difficulty.
So far as the government is concerned, I think we have to have a recess because it has not the legislation ready that has been requested. I think the Leader of the Opposition has his tongue in his cheek when he asks for the pension legislation to be brought forth immediately. There has not been time to prepare it. The government has been busy doing other things.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: Does the hon. member know we asked for this legislation to be brought forward weeks ago, as did his colleague, the whip of his party?

Of course we have been pressing hard for this over a long period of time; but from the answers given by the government it is clear that the legislation is not prepared, and the only way it can be prepared is to give the cabinet a month or six weeks holiday in which to prepare it.
The legislation which was introduced concerning student loans was terrible legislation, poorly and improperly drafted, indicating terrific haste. I suggest the government needs a recess, but the Prime Minister has gone on television and made some asinine statements which he really did not understand, which he

really did not document; and we are now faced with a continuation of the type of abuse that is taking place in parliament while we wait for the two protagonists to make up their minds on what they are going to do about it. I have no objection to its being three months rather than two months, or it can be granted until the end of the year. It looks now as though this government, along with others in previous years, has decided that the estimates do not really mean estimates, but public accounts. We have been discussing estimates long after the year to which they referred has gone by. Governments should take a look at this matter before they ask for interim supply.
The President of the Privy Council who is asking for this extension today is perhaps the person best qualified to tell the committee about the whole program covered by the estimates, and what discussion of the estimates means in a democratic country. He is well aware of the situation and has made statements about the principles involved on many occasions. I think that in asking today for three months' supply, without making a commitment that some real result of benefit will follow either for members of this committee or for the country, he is being unfair. We are placed in the position of being pawns in a game which we are not playing at all but which is being played outside this chamber at the present time.

1 would simply say that the proposal I placed before the committee, as I pointed out last night, was not based on information from any of the leaders or from any of the leaders' meetings, but based on suggestions made here in the committee of the whole house. It was put forward by the Leader of the Opposition and supported by other hon. members.
I do not wish to develop the subject, because I see it is almost five o'clock. ["Mr. Speaker, in approaching debate on a bill of this kind, which in its short form is entitled the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Revision Act, 1964, it is possible of course to become almost inextricably involved with statistics, and as debate moves about from one side of the house to the other or from one member to another there can be a very extensive selection of statistics proving a great many points of view but not perhaps acceptable to all points of view. Therefore I shall endeavour, in what I have to say now -if I can have enough silence to be heard at all-to avoid statistical references and deal with one or two principles that are involved in this bill.
One of these principles has been mentioned already this evening by two of the previous speakers. It was referred to on an earlier occasion, at the resolution stage by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Willoughby), and it was referred to again tonight by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) and also the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson). This is the question with respect to the assessment of income from natural resources in a province as part of the basis of establishing the province's participation in equalization payments. There has to be, as was suggested previously and again tonight, some consideration given to the question of the nature of this income, for obviously part of the income from the natural resources of a province is drawn from", 'Federal-Provincial Relations non-renewable resources, from minerals, oil and natural gas. The income is being derived from a wasting resource. There is nothing the province or anyone can do to renew that resource. Once it is gone, it is gone forever. Once it has been used, there will be no further income from it; there will be no renewal of income from that particular resource-it has been expended.
Therefore to take into account revenue as a consequence of a sale of that resource as part of the income of a province is undoubtedly dangerous. Serious consideration should be given by the federal government to some formula by which a province is credited with the depletion of its resources. Unless such a depletion allowance is provided in the consideration of income of the province, this formula is not fair and is not equitable. There are other resources, forest resources and water resources, that can be used, renewed and used again. There, again, it is not equitable that the province should be charged with all the income derived from those resources in considering its share of tax equalization payments, because obviously these renewable resources must be managed.
Each province must spend a substantial amount of money annually in renewing its forest resources, protecting and to a substantial extent renewing and perpetuating, through some measures that can be taken in some provinces, its water resources. These are charges upon the province which do not appear in the equation as indicated in this bill. If there is to be equity in the consideration of the economic wealth of the provinces, these factors must be taken into account by the federal government. There must be this recognition of depreciation of non-renewable resources, and recognition of the cost of perpetuating and preserving renewable resources.
I trust that the minister, when he comes to answer the comments made, will have some understanding of what I have just said, as I notice he is paying not the slightest attention. These factors have not been taken into account in any statement made by the government. The minister has not even caught up with my latest intervention, but I hope he will later.
I submit these factors must be taken into account if there is to be an equitable sharing of financial resources in the provinces. If the provinces are to have the responsibility for and the cost of administering, protecting and preserving their resources, the federal government in taking revenue from them and the provinces being required, in effect,
[Mr. Fleming (Okanagan-Revelstoke).l
to share that revenue with the federal government, the costs to the provinces must be taken into account by the federal government before it makes its assessment. I think that is fundamental and applies to any business. You simply do not milk your assets till they are gone and there is no asset left with which to produce future revenue. Any business can be destroyed pretty fast by not taking into account depreciation of assets. In the income tax and corporation tax structure of the federal government depreciation must be taken into account, and it must be taken into account in this formula which has been established by the federal government in arriving at which of the provinces shall not participate in equalization payments. The formula must also take into account that this will work to the benefit of some provinces which now benefit substantially from equalization payments and at the same time are provinces which can derive substantial revenue from the sale of natural resources. Such provinces might benefit from this consideration as well as provinces like British Columbia and Alberta, which find that their natural resource income deprives them of the right of participation in equalization payments under the present formula.
Another matter which has been mentioned many times in the house, both in the course of the resolution debate and also this evening, so therefore I will not labour the point, is that an equally important point with regard to this federal-provincial fiscal revision act does not appear in the bill. It is something which is absent from this bill but has not been absent from the considerations of this house during the past few days. It is an indication of government policy on sharing the cost of highway building in the provinces.
Late in July the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) indicated that this fall there is to be a dominion-provincial conference on national highways policy. Naturally no one would argue with the necessity for such a conference; members from every province would welcome one. But it was assumed that at that time there would be a general assessment of the federal role in highway construction in the provinces, whether the federal government had in fact any role or responsibility at all. It could be assumed that when this announcement was made about this conference, federal government participation in road building programs in the provinces on a major scale would wait until after the conference. That might be one

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
reason why this particular aspect of federal-provincial co-operation is not included in this bill.
Within the past 48 hours-in fact yesterday-we found that although there is to be a highways conference in the fall the government has come to an ad hoc arrangement with one of the provinces and decided to spend $13 million on a purely provincial road. It is not even a road which could be considered in the national context. It might have come within the general context of roads to resources or even forest access roads, but we know that the present administration has eliminated both those programs and they are gone. Therefore we cannot find any over-all national policy to account for this sudden, one-shot roadbuilding program introduced in one province.
I am not arguing against the merits of such a program but I am arguing against this ad hoc arrangement, this one-shot deal undertaken in the face of what we had assumed would be federal government policy to consult with all the provinces to arrive at a national highways policy. Then when one is confronted with this bill and finds that it provides that a province like British Columbia is not to participate to any extent in tax equalization programs, and when one finds that the roads to resources and forest access programs have been discontinued and no other provision made for a joint federal-provincial roadbuilding program, which is of tremendous importance, if not of vital necessity, to the provinces, it is clear this bill has been circumvented in this sudden, one-shot, ad hoc arrangement with one of the provinces. This is in defiance of the very principles established in the bill and contained in other government statements, including that of the Minister of Public Works, relating to a national highways program.
In view of the fact that there seems to be plenty of precedent in the house tonight for a member speaking on behalf of his own province and perhaps considering provincial interests over national interests, I must say that it seems to me that this is something which is being thrust upon us by the provisions of this bill and the announcement made yesterday, coupled with the inadequacy of federal policy in regard to British Columbia, the particular problems of communications in that province and the absolute necessity for federal interest in highways policy as it applies to the west coast in particular. In this regard I refer to the necessity for linking the Pacific coast of Canada more satisfactorily with the rest of Canada through direct highway access to the seaports on the coast.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is it the pleasure of the house to adopt the said motion?
Explain.

Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege for me to bring Bill No. S-6 to the attention of all hon. members. As the representative of Winnipeg South and a lifelong resident of that city whose family and forefathers pioneered in western Canada, I consider this occasion a great honour.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) has said in this house that the government is not opposed to further competition in the banking field. In fact, he has indicated that more competition in banking, as in other fields, would be welcome provided three conditions were met. Any new bank, he said, must first be adequately financed; second, it must be supported by financially responsible people; and third, provision should be made for retaining control in Canada. I would like to take these points one by one. First, a new bank must be adequately financed. The Bank of Western Canada, if incorporated, expects to be able to commence business with $13 million in capital and rest account, which would be the largest amount any Canadian chartered bank has had at its beginning. Rather than merely indicating the intention to raise $13 million, it was decided to obtain
[The Chairman.]
these funds on a trusteed basis pending the granting of a charter. Should a charter not be granted, the funds would be returned to would-be subscribers.
At this time I do not want to go into all the details of the financing of this bank as I am hoping that all questions will be answered in committee. Briefly, though, the capital stock of the bank will be $10 million divided into one million shares of $10 par. In addition to the 100 initial subscribers of stock listed as incorporators in Bill No. S-6, there are now 6,000 Canadian residents holding trustee subscription certificates entitling them to subscribe for stock in the new bank if and when incorporated by parliament. I would say that the Bank of 'Western Canada will be adequately financed.
The second point was, a bank should be supported by financially responsible people. In clause 1 of this bill hon. members will see the names of the 100 individuals who have joined together to be petitioners in the application for incorporation of the bank. Eighty five per cent of them are residents of the four western provinces and 15 per cent are from Ontario. About 60 per cent of the total petitioners are businessmen in these areas, but there are also physicians, lawyers, chartered accountants, university professors, farmers, engineers, journalists, pharmacists and other occupational groups. I can assure the house that this is a very representative list and I believe that all these people will be of great help in organizing the bank. The directors of the proposed bank will be drawn from this list, and other persons active in Canada's economic life. The majority will be resident in the west.
The third point the Minister of Finance made was that there should be retaining control in Canada. I believe that the Bank of Western Canada will be truly all-Canadian. No foreign participation will be accepted in the formation of the bank. The pre-incorporation offering prospectus made it clear that this stock may not be purchased by non-residents of Canada. Each subscriber has been requested to sign a statement which would ensure that ownership of shares can only be held by Canadian residents and cannot be transferred to a non-resident or any person acting as a nominee, agent, trustee or on behalf of a non-resident. The applicant must be a person ordinarily resident in Canada, or a company incorporated under the laws of Canada or of a province of Canada, and one which has its principal place of business in

Canada, and is not by any means whatsoever under the control of non-residents of Canada.
I would like to draw the attention of the house to clause 5, subclause 3 of this bill, which spells out the restrictions of transfers of shares to non-residents, the total aggregate of which may never exceed 10 per cent of the total number of shares then issued and outstanding. Again I say, Mr. Speaker, that the Bank of Western Canada will be truly all-Canadian.
Now, why has this request for a new bank been made? Certainly the petitioners have no grievance with any of the existing banks in Canada. They believe that our banking principles have been the backbone of our excellent Canadian banking system, which enjoys a world-wide reputation for soundness and stability. But times have changed, even since 1963. I would like to give the house some of the basic reasons why I believe there should be a Bank of Western Canada. First there is the extraordinary economic growth of Canada, particularly western Canada. This growth needs an increase in the banking institutions to serve that economy. In 1954 Canada had 11 chartered banks; now, in 1964, there are only eight. I think I am right when I say that the gross national product of Canada has almost doubled in those last ten years; I think the figures are, from $25 billion to $43 billion.
I believe that western Canada should have a bank with its head office, with its seat of control and management, in western Canada. It seems ridiculous that no bank has its head office west of Toronto. Only in this way will the financial needs of western Canada receive the close attention and understanding they deserve. Then I believe that the economy of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia is sufficiently varied and broadly based to support a western Canadian bank without having to go to the capital markets of Toronto, Montreal or New York.
The capital needs for the western provinces are sufficiently important to the people living there to warrant their asking parliament to incorporate a bank specially devoted to the development of this part of our country. What I heartily approve of is that the Bank of Western Canada would have modest branches operating in an economical and efficient way with concentration on small and medium sized accounts. In this way I believe the Bank of Western Canada would fill a growing need for a regional financial institution to take care of regional economic
Private Bills
development. The interprovincial co-operation between the four western provinces in the development of water resources, power, irrigation and mineral growth point to the need for such a financial institution. It should be based in the west and geared to the business opportunities that are developing in this vast and exciting area. The headquarters of this Bank of Western Canada would be in Winnipeg.
Hon. members, I believe the incorporators of this bank have shown great foresight and initiative in all their planning. Six weeks after they had made application for their charter, the report of the Porter royal commission on banking was tabled here in this house, namely on April 24. So many of the ideas they had had when drawing up this bill have been expressed in this massive document. The Porter report has recommended a more open and competitive banking system in Canada. It has referred to the dangers of undue concentration. Allow me to quote a few of its passages relating to competition in banking. This passage is to be found at page 362:
There must be sufficient competition among these institutions that borrowers and savers have alternatives open to them.
Then again at pages 367 and 368:
It is undoubtedly true that in banking, as in other business, there are advantages in being big and in being able to provide specialized services in many fields. However, there are disadvantages as well and we do not subscribe to the view that size alone will give the banks a necessary advantage. . .In any event, there is no reason why smaller banks and other institutions cannot compete successfully for all other types of business: indeed they may handle large accounts by splitting them among a number of smaller institutions.
Then at page 375 the commission make this recommendation:
We have therefore recommended the continuance of certain features of the present act, and the introduction of others, with a view to ensuring that competition is not blunted by price agreements or the uncontrolled acquisition of competing institutions by their rivals.
My final quotation is from page 564:
We have, in summary, favoured a more open and competitive banking system-carefully and fairly regulated under uniform legislation but not bound by restrictions which impede response of the institutions to new situations-
The Bank of Western Canada fits into this pattern. The sponsors realize that business opportunities in western Canada deserve special attention. Such a bank would give western residents encouragement to mobilize their own capital resources for investment in

Private Bills
the opportunities they see around them and a chance to develop new and imaginative ideas.
Hon. members, I hope there will be no delay of this bill to incorporate the bank of western Canada. Today's Bank Act on the statute books applies to the incorporation of a new bank. Bill S-6 complies with the Bank Act as it now stands. Under the Bank Act parliament has a duty to consider each applicant seeking to incorporate a new bank on that applicant's merits.
I urge you all to allow this bill to go before our parliamentary standing committee on banking and commerce, where all the most technical questions will be answered. We, particularly those of us from western Canada, look forward to the day we can show in a tangible way our enthusiasm for this proposed new bank. It has been heartily endorsed by so many. Let us give these Canadians an opportunity to assist our banking system to meet the needs of our growing and increasingly international young country.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to say very briefly that we in the Social Credit party have no objection to sending this bill to the standing committee on banking and commerce. It is well known to all hon. members of this house that we do take some objection to the way the banks in this country are operated today, but we do not believe that it would serve our purpose to restrict the number of banks in the country. We are happy to note that the Bank Act will be coming before the committee of the House of Commons some time later this year, we hope, and certainly not later than June 30 next year, at which time we will have an opportunity to state our objections to the present situation and to suggest some changes to the act. However, Mr. Speaker, I make it abundantly clear that this bank, if it comes into existence, along with other existing banks would of course be subjected to the rules and changes which will be made when the Bank Act is before this house.
I think the report of the Porter commission, to which the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mrs. Konantz) referred a number of times, indicates that the chartered banks in this country have failed in many respects to provide the kind of credit facilities demanded by the Canadian people. This is manifest by the growth of what have been termed "near banks", treasury branches, credit unions, and so on. We will be making a detailed examination of this failure and the changes which are necessary to meet the demands of the Canadian people when the Bank Act is before

the house and the committee. In the meantime we have no objection to sending this bill to our standing committee.

Mr. Speaker, before coming to the few principles I intend to set forth before the house concerning Bill No. S-6, I must congratulate the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mrs. Konantz) for the excellent statement she made in order to justify the existence of this new bank, when she referred to the necessary competition in the banking field.
But considering that we already have had more than 30 different banks in Canada and that, during the last 60 years those banks have been centralized into eight banks, I am wondering whether one is justified today in requesting a decentralization, through the creation or incorporation of new banks, as a means of solving banking credit and monetary problems in this country.
And, by an irony of fate, I find among the 100 representatives, as pointed out by the hon. member for Winnipeg South, the name of Mr. James Coyne.
It will surely be recalled that in 1954, when he was governor of the Bank of Canada, Mr. Coyne told us, Canadians, through the press-and you remember that some of his statements were discussed in this house: You, Canadians, have been living beyond your means for the past 15 years and the time has come to tighten your belts. He was then announcing a tight money policy.
No attention was paid to the fact that, in 1954, Canada could produce a great deal of useful goods, consumer goods or services to accommodate its people. But the financial structure led Mr. Coyne to tell us that we should do without certain things and tighten our belts, because we had been living beyond our means.
In fact, this restrictive credit policy was established. We witnessed its disastrous results, reflected in a slowdown of the economic business of our country, in 1955, 1956 and 1957, years which followed the advice to restrict credit given to the chartered banks. That policy caused such a slowdown that unemployment settled in our country as an awful plague.
Already, in 1957 and 1958, discussions took place in the House of Commons in order to seek a solution to the unemployment problem.
I am not saying that the whole problem is due to the tight money policy recommended by Mr. Coyne in 1954, but I hold it to be one

of the major causes of that economic slowdown which created the depression and the unemployment which prevailed during those years.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I have been listening with much interest during the past few minutes to the comments made by the hon. member for Beauce and I wonder if he is not straying too far away from the bill before us.
I think his comments are not directly related to the bill before us and I would ask him to co-operate with the other members of the house in restricting his remarks to the legislation before the house.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I was just going to explain how credit restrictions can have ill effects on a country's economy and end up by giving the reasons why we are opposed to the issuance of a charter which would allow this banking system which has led us to economic stagnation to go on.
Since parliament is being asked to authorize the issue of a bank charter, I feel it is only normal that we should examine a little the economy's activities in relation to banking.
I have precisely given as an example the 1954 credit restrictions.
In 1957 and 1960, we were not the only ones to criticize those restrictions, as a matter of fact, statements made by certain professors and economists led to the resignation of Mr. Coyne, who was then governor of the Bank of Canada. Therefore, such a policy had repercussions, not only according to the Social Credit people, but also to those economists who realized that the banking system, as applied under directives from the Bank of Canada, was not adapted to the needs of the Canadian nation.
The following reason could also be given: that bank will operate under the Bank Act now in force in Canada.
The Bank Act will probably be amended next year as a result of the report of the commission which for several years has been studying the improvements which should be made to the said act, but in accordance with the present banking system.
Now let us consider the results of that system: Canadians are now in debt for over $72 billion. This fact, Mr. Speaker, is mentioned in the report of the commission on banking activities in this country which points out that the total debts of Canadians which now reach $72 billion are divided as follows:
Private Bills
Government of Canada: $19.4 billion in 1962.
Provinces: $9 billion in 1962
Business: $4.3 billion
Commercial credit: $14 billion
Mortgage loans: $5.4 billion
Consumers: $14 billion.
Personally, I am not prepared to make it easier to secure new bank charters because I see banks as leeches sucking the economic blood of the nation, leading and controlling it in its economic activities.
I am surprised to see, in this day and age, when practically the world over there is talk of nationalization-nationalization of power, nationalization of forests, nationalization of mines, nationalization of everything that can be big, nationalization of telephone service- that nobody talks of nationalizing credit institutions and yet 90 per cent of the economic activities of the individuals who make up the nation depend on them.
Nowadays, some people are ready to nationalize or put under state control everything, except the greatest of all trusts.
That reminds me of those who want to get rid of vermin but who continue to feed handsomely the breeding stock that bring forth vermin. They do exactly the same thing; they denounce trusts of all sorts, economic and financial interests which control everything, through easy access to credit, thanks to means made available to them by our banking system as a whole-either by trust associations or by means of rights granted under the Bank Act to multiply the deposits in the form of banking credit-but they allow the mother of all trusts to continue breeding more trusts.
People even go so far as asking that others be added to the existing ones.
Therefore, with regard to the bill before us and to the remarks of the hon. member who preceded me, I realize that it is meant to favour competition.
I said just now that we have had more than three kinds of banks in Canada. Indebtedness rose, and even multiplied steadily so that today we cannot but wonder who really controls Canada. In the same way we may wonder who really controls some of the provinces.
Those who control the country are not the politicians responsible for government administration. In many cases they are not actually responsible, but those who have taken control of the money and credit and,

Private Bills
therefore, of our economy and all opportunities of some scope-or rather of the immense possibilities-offered by this country's natural wealth.
I am certainly not one to like compromise or half-measures. I admit that, under the present system, this might favour some economic development in the west. But it would only be at the expense of some other development, or mean a strengthening of a few people's centralizing power even if there was only a hundred of them.
It is all very well to demand that all shareholders be residents of Canada. But whether one is exploited by a Canadian resident or a foreign resident through a system leading to rack and ruin, which prevents Canadians, because of their economic system, from attaining the highest possible degree of prosperity in a political, economic and cultural order and freedom which is everybody's goal in this world-what does it matter?
We are the only ones to denounce it. Though we belong to the Social Credit movement, we do not want to see other private business controlling the issue of money and credit. Indeed we consider that such control over money and credit, whether in the form of script money, paper money or coins, must not be left in private hands because we consider money as the most social instrument needed by society.
Whoever we may be we all depend on money in that field. However abundant production by the great trusts may be-whether they represent private enterprise or co-operative business-the ownership and volume of goods becomes a question of service which must reach the consumer.
Why? Because the monetary system requires it. It is because discretionary powers were centralized in the hands of some group which today rules the destiny of peoples in a way which runs counter to their true spirit because they want in no way to follow that course.
I have before me some remarks which were made by authors who, though being experts in economy none the less are not crediters but who, mind you, indicate that credit in society should not be left in the hands of private enterprise.
I believe that too often, alas, when we deal with monetary questions, as is the case today, when we are studying this bill, the object of which is a charter intended for a bank-we see no better principle-first of all there are two main factors which must be taken into account in the question of credit.

First of all, there is the real credit based on productive and consumptive capacity. Such is real credit, that which can be called the credit of society. The real credit of the Canadian society is what it is able, as a whole, through its technical knowledge, its natural resources, its political, economic, cultural and social development, to develop and to give in the largest possible measure, to the smaller and even to the younger member of society, the real credit of the Canadian nation.
At the present time, how many companies, private enterprise or co-operatives cannot develop normally on account of credit restrictions imposed by the banks? To my mind there is not a shadow of a doubt about it.
There is quite a difference between real credit and bank credit. That is why we say that the credit of society must be turned into money, not by private enterprises, but by a social credit agency or by an agency responsible to society, which will look after credit facilities in areas needing such credit.
I have before me an extract from a book entitled "The Economic Doctrine of the Church", by Dauphin Meunier, in which he points out the disadvantages of the creation of bank credit by private banks. Here is what he says:
Modem commercial banks accept deposits only to use them, they borrow only to lend to production. These operations were done and undone by way of mere entries in the books, without the use of coin or paper money, which shows that banks have at their disposal a new power, that of issuing what the Belgian economist Anciault called script money.
When we know that today 90 to 92 per cent of economic activities in Canada are done by way of script money, through credit-debit columns, transferred from one branch to another in the various banks operating in Canada, is this not proof that our nation's economic activity is controlled by our eight chartered banks?
Indeed, during the contradictory debate which went on in 1954 and in 1960, Mr. James Coyne, one of those who applied for this bank charter, threw the blame on the chartered banks to which Mr. James Weir, the then chairman of the Canadian Banking Association replied: "How can we be held responsible when we have to borrow from the Bank of Canada at a rate exceeding 5 per cent, and we are limited to a rate of 6 per cent on our loans?" However, he did not say that the banks could increase their credit eight to 10 times, thus getting $600 in interest on a $1,000 deposit because they could create ten times that amount through bank credit.

It was such statements which created such a mess of confusion and which, after two years of debate, brought about the resignation of Mr. James Coyne as governor of the Bank of Canada. And the then minister of finance, Mr. Fleming, found out all about credit restrictions.
We are not the only ones, therefore, to deplore this fact. Today, there is some talk of nationalizing everything in the best interests of individuals and of social progress. On the other hand, when the banking system is referred to as the most powerful of all trusts and of all economic forces that may exist in any country, how is it possible then to think of granting a further bank charter?
There are surely some reasons to object to such a decision, at least until a more complete study of the report submitted following an investigation on banking activities has shown that it is the only or the best way to promote the development of certain areas in our country. Therefore, I do not think we have to pass immediately the incorporation of a bank for western Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I realize that, in certain quarters, it will be said that we are against economic development, against credit facilities and economic expansion in the western provinces. On the contrary, we hope that, as soon as possible, at least the two provinces now headed by premiers who say they are promoters of Social Credit will demand, at federal-provincial conferences, the revision of the banking policy of this country in order that, through the Bank of Canada, or even through the provincial governments, a real system of exchange, easier and more in line with the needs of our time, more consistent with the facts of the 20th century, shall be set up and that discretionary powers shall not be further centralized through the banks.
For those reasons, before I conclude my remarks, I move seconded by Mr. Laprise, member for Chapleau:
That Eill No. S-6 be not now read a second time, but that it be deferred six months.

We, Social Crediters, have had enough of the banking system which piles debts upon debts. The hon. member for Beauce pointed out a while ago that, according to the report of the Porter commission on banking and finance, our debt amounted to $72 billion. However, that assertion might not be absolutely accurate because even then, they forgot to mention the deposits in banks which, after all, are debts, and it would mean that our total debt, at this time, adds up to $90 billion.
Mr. Speaker, for 100 years our country was continuously pushed into debt because, at the beginning of confederation, in 1867, the national debt amounted to only $93 million, and thanks to our good old banking system, the same debt now amounts to $22 billion. Therefore, it is crystal clear that we could not approve of such a system.
Personally, as a Social Crediter I have endeavoured for at least 20 years to have that system changed, and it is a sure thing that I would not take the liberty to authorize an extension of the system.
Mr. Speaker, I am against that bill because it gives to the bank discretionary powers and it gives to the bankers powers that are absolutely contrary to the welfare of the population. It is absolutely contrary to public interest and I gave evidence of that a minute ago when I mentioned the continued growth of our debt.
Power is granted to bankers-under the Bank Act-to create money and credit, and

these are the people who actually govern today.
In fact, our leaders, from whatever government or level of government they are, either federal, provincial or municipal, or member of school boards, are subject to our financial system, which decides whether there will be crisis or prosperity. However, when a war breaks out, it is still through the same financial system that it is found possible to put into circulation millions of dollars when it is impossible to find dollars to help our Canadian families.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member allow me a question?
Yes, Mr. Speaker.
Mr. Speaker, is the hon. member saying that the setting up of a financial system in accordance with the Social Credit formula would have the effect of abolishing all the debts in the world?

Mr. Speaker, one would show very little intelligence in pretending such a thing. But there is a difference between having a system which is always accumulating debts, and creating a provisional debt. A debt is something that must exist.
To what extent would debts be reduced under your system?

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member for Lotbiniere wishes to have a full account of the Social Credit doctrine, he just has to wait a few moments, I can give it to him. If what I say is not sufficient, he only has to come to my office and I will spend another hour to explain it to him, but I doubt very much that he would be able to understand.
Nobody can understand it.

There are none so deaf as those that will not hear.
When we explain our theories on Social Credit, no opponent of ours ever stands up with figures in his hands to prove that he is right. Indeed, we are not the only ones to say so.
For the time being, I merely wish to explain how the banks came to wield such enormous power.
Allow me to quote a single section of the Bank Act which gives them such power. I refer to section 71 (1) which provides:
The bank shall maintain a cash reserve In the form of a deposit with the Bank of Canada and of Bank of Canada notes held by the bank, and such reserve shall be not less on the average during
	-
any month than 8 per cent, or such other percentage as may be fixed by the Bank of Canada under the provisions of the Bank of Canada Act, of such of its deposit liabilities as are payable in Canadian currency.
In simpler terms, or in overly simple terms, this means what? That as long as the bank has a deposit of $8, it can lend up to $100.
I know that.
You know it and you are satisfied that bankers are allowed to do this, that is with $8 they can lend $100 at 6 per cent interest?
To the government, for instance.

Yes, to the government.
What would the hon. member for Lotbiniere say if he knew of a baker who, in order to sell bread, would borrow it from his neighbour instead of baking it himself? He would say he is a simpleton. That is what the government is doing at present.
Banks are obliged to have a reserve of 8 per cent. But that is not all; there is more to it than that. They accumulate another 7 per cent reserve, thus making a total reserve of 15 per cent.
This means that whenever you make a deposit of $1,000, the bank places $150 aside as a reserve. It can use the $850 which remain as a reserve and it can multiply that amount by 10; then it can lend $8,500 at 6 per cent. That is the way it can make a profit.
If the hon. member for Lotbiniere does not feel that this is a racket, I do not know how we can call it.
That makes 60 per cent interest.

Lending institutions in Canada are blamed because they charge interest rates up to 32 per cent, while the bank itself charges at least 54 per cent on its loans, if everything is taken into consideration. When the bank lends you $100 at 6 per cent interest, mind you, it has only $10. Therefore, if it charges $6 for $10, that makes 54 per cent.

speechtext:
I want to deal briefly at this stage of the bill with some general matters affecting the federal relationship with the provinces, and then to deal more specifically with the situation as I see it in Alberta. A good deal has been said with regard to the situation in which Alberta finds itself and I think the position should be straightened out.
First I wish to say something with regard to the general confederation picture. The fiscal arrangements between the federal government and the provinces are the very core around which our federal system has to operate. I am one who believes that if we are to have a strong country we need a strong central government. This is not to say the provinces should not have and maintain the rights which are theirs under the British North America Act. However, we must be careful that we do not set up in Canada ten local potentates and give them the money with which to operate local countries on a lavish scale. I think we are bound to have regard to the taxpayer who, after all, will have to pay the shot, whether through federal taxes or provincial taxes, however the tax revenues are shared between federal and provincial governments.
I think the meeting of the premiers held recently in my riding underlined certain of the problems we are facing at this stage of confederation. Among them is the situation we are getting into with regard to trade between provinces. Surely we will not reach a position where there are trade barriers at every provincial boundary. We need a strong central government to make sure there is a free flow of goods from one province to another. Again there is the question of the location of industry. Surely we must not allow ourselves to get into a situation where one province tries to rob another, or attempts to attract new industries at the expense of its neighbours. Thus the central government is bound to maintain a strong position, particularly with regard to fiscal matters. It has to be the leader in these fields so that the provinces may know where they stand and so that they can all act together to build a vigorous and healthy Canada.
This need for leadership at the federal level affects almost every facet of our daily

Federal-Provincial Relations lives-health, education, industrial development, trade, even the basic liberties of the individual. In past years, the government led by my right hon. friend, the member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) did a great deal to satisfy some of the demands of the provinces for increased revenue to meet their increased responsibilities and enable them to deal with the "growing pains" which all of them are experiencing. Bill No. C-lll proposes to make certain changes in the fiscal arrangements with the provinces and to provide adjustments-the so-called equalization provisions-to bring the "have not" provinces up to the level of the two richest provinces. We in Alberta, of course, will not get anything from these equalization provisions, since they are drawn up so as to take into consideration revenue from natural resources-revenue from resources which are being sold off, and which represent the sale of an asset rather than continuing revenue from an asset. Even though the government which happens to be in power in Alberta today does not regard it as such, and seems to think on occasion that it does not really matter what they do with their money, the good Lord is going to look after them, in that they do not have to finance like the rest of the provinces. They have spread across our province and into the province immediately west of us-and they would like to get the idea across Canada- that debt is a very bad thing. Certainly it is a very bad thing if you do not have the assets with which to back it up.
While talking about debt, I think it might be worth while, particularly with regard to the situation in Alberta and the need for increased revenues for the provinces, if I mentioned that one of the big factors, of course, has been the division of the revenue the province receives down further to the municipal level. We have heard in this house on occasion some talk with regard to the amount of debt there is in the provinces of Alberta and British Columbia. I am not going to say too much with regard to the situation in British Columbia, other than that they have done the same thing there, of course; they have transferred the debt from the province to crown corporations and it becomes an indirect debt, but it is still a direct charge against the province. I understand that in British Columbia they have managed to increase their debt by a billion dollars in the last six or seven years.
In the province of Alberta in particular we have the situation at the moment whereby our municipal government is weighed down

by a tax structure which is higher than anywhere else in Canada. The net per capita, municipal debt-according to the Canada Year Book for the latest year I can find-in Alberta is higher than any other province in Canada. In other words, in Alberta they have a far higher municipal debt, per capita, than in any other province of Canada. I would like to put some of these figures on the record, because sometimes they get a little clouded. In Alberta the per capita municipal debt-that is, including the debt of the municipalities and school districts-amounts to $360. In British Columbia it is $270; in Ontario, $280; in Quebec, $302. The other provinces are well below 200 per capita in municipal debt. I want to repeat Alberta's figure; it is $360 per capita, which is quite a bit higher than it is in any other province in Canada.
One of the problems we have in Alberta, then, is to do something to see that this extra money which is going to go to them out of Bill No. C-lll gets down to the local government level, in order to help relieve them of the crushing debt which the property owners in Alberta are now carrying. They are carrying it themselves, in their own names, because the province of Alberta of course has a very strong psychological feeling against going into debt on its own. This is, of course, just fooling the people in this regard. One of the results is that the property tax in Alberta is extremely high. I have not been able to find any comparative rates, but I am sure it is as high as or higher than it is in any other province in Canada. The two big factors in this high debt and this high tax rate are these -property owners in Alberta are paying for health and education. In most of our counties, towns and municipalities the municipal tax rate is relatively normal; but our educational tax rate is high, and of course we are the only province in Canada which imposes a property tax for hospital purposes.
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), earlier, at the resolution stage, talked about co-insurance, which I will deal with in a moment. But we are still the only province in Canada which finances part of its hospitalization program by means of a direct property tax of at least 4 mills, an additional mill for public health and an additional mill for chronic hospitals. We have in Alberta all this burden dumped directly back on to the property owner. We are hoping that with this additional money which is to become available to the provinces, the premier of the province of Alberta will see fit to relieve

some of this crushing debt on the municipalities and take over the entire basic costs of education and health, which the municipalities are now paying. We see no reason why our property owners should pay income tax as well; why their share of this increased income tax which is going to go to the provinces should not be used to relieve this crushing debt.
The Michener report published in Manitoba recently gives, I think, a guide to some of our provinces in this regard. We certainly need to do something to relieve the very difficult situation in which our municipalities, counties, towns and cities find themselves in the province of Alberta, even though our provincial government, with its very large resource revenue, has not had too much difficulty. The hon. member for Red Deer also mentioned a revolving loan fund which he thought was still in existence. I am sure he has not been in Alberta very much of late, because in 1956 or 1957 they scrapped their municipal loan fund and set up a crown corporation to borrow money on the outside money market and re-lend it to the municipalities.
Of course, the money this municipal financing corporation borrows is not a debt of the province, if you listen to them; the province only guarantees the debentures that the M.F.C. sells. If this is not a direct debt of the province, I would like to know what is. A similar situation exists with regard to the telephone system under the Alberta government, and some other crown corporations in Alberta are borrowing money, as any crown corporation or other corporation would that required capital; they have been borrowing both inside and outside Canada. To suggest that the province of Alberta is debt free is just nonsense.
There is another question which should also be looked into; that is, whether or not the federal government should have some control over the fiscal lending policies of our provincial governments. I am not so sure that it has been a wise thing for the province of Alberta to refrain from getting itself into debt, particularly at times when it could have borrowed money at a very good rate of interest, for the development of our province. They failed to do this then and instead said, "We are going to pay our way". We are only paying our way because we are selling off part of our resources. This is not a recurring resource; it is only recurring in so far as the markets for oil, gas and the by-products of the petroleum industry are available, and it is
Federal^Provincial Relations only recurring in so far as exploration causes new fields to be found which will build up the resource of the province. Once this oil, gas and other by-products are sold off, it is gone; it is not a continuing resource. We feel very strongly that we are being penalized because of the policy of our provincial government to sell off our resources.
I should now like to say a few words about the equalization formula. Of course, our per capita, maximum income is something like $90, which is very much more than any other province in Canada, so Alberta does not enter into the equalization formula at all. I want to say one or two more words with regard to education. It was said during the debate on the resolution stage that there should be a federal department of education. I feel strongly that one of the things that a federal or central government should do is to oversee and to set standards of education for the provinces to meet, and I fail to see where this would infringe, or interfere with provincial autonomy. Another matter which we in western Canada have always felt with regard to provincial autonomy, and which I would throw out as a suggestion to my hon. friends from Quebec, is this, that the federal government should have a check rein on any local potentate who might want to take over a province. If the provinces are given too much local autonomy there is no one who would be able to stand up for the civil rights of the individual within that province.
Again I think that a federal standard of education applied across Canada would not impinge upon any provincial autonomy and might give us a basic standard in the most economical manner; and certainly with the continuing cost of education this will need to be provided as economically as possible. In Alberta, as I say, the total cost of education amounts to $100 million a year, and we hope that the government of Alberta will take the additional money given to them over the next two years under this bill in order to assume the entire cost of education, as it has now gone beyond the stage where the provincial government or local governments can properly finance it.
One other comment regarding health and hospitalization, and the co-insurance fee. Being involved in the health profession I am in favour of the co-insurance fee as a deterrent to unnecessary hospitalization. I see nothing wrong with it and I hope that the federal government will take a further look at the situation in Alberta so that the people in that province will not be penalized as they

Federal-Provincial Relations have in the past-as a matter of fact since the implementation of the national hospitalization act. We think that the co-insurance deterrent fee is justified and see nothing wrong with such a deterrent fee. We think it is worth while; it works out in practical terms and it helps prevent unnecessary hospitalization. If a province wants to take the initiative for such a measure then I do not think it should be penalized.
They are some of the main points, Mr. Speaker, regarding this bill. Again I point out that we in Alberta are very strong-minded toward a one Canada approach, toward a strong central government, keeping in mind that our provincial government has to have the autonomy to run the affairs within its boundaries. On hearing one hon. member talk of the plight of farmers in eastern Canada I could not help but think that we in western Canada would have been in a sorry state had we not had a very strong federal government at the time to which we could make representations over the years on behalf of western agriculture. Perhaps one of the reasons that the eastern farmer, particularly in Quebec, is in this plight is because he has allowed his quest for provincial autonomy to be so much uppermost in his mind that he has not felt like making representations in a forceful manner to the central government. One of the reasons for having a central government is that it should play the role of overseer and make sure that each part of our country is coming along on relatively the same scale. That of course is done by way of equalization payments, something with which we do not disagree as we showed during the years we were in office.
We believe in the equalization system. However, I think all hon. members will agree that equalization is a temporary method, which has to be reviewed at regular intervals so that the government grants can be adjusted, because our provinces do not develop at the same rate. Certainly an equalization program is at best only a temporary measure; the objective we have to work for in Canada is the provision of equal opportunities for all people in the country, so that each one of our provinces can develop itself to the utmost and will not need this additional help from the central government. I think that should be our aim.
With those few remarks, Mr. Speaker, may I say we are of course willing to support Bill No. C-lll.
