First of all, these figures show that there are only two provinces in Canada, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island, which receive more money by way of equalization payments than is collected in taxes. Therefore it is quite incorrect to say, as the hon. member for Lapointe said, that there are only two provinces in Canada which pay more in taxes than they get back. All provinces except Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland pay or have collected within their borders more in taxes than they receive back in equalization payments.
But I think hon. members will find that the interesting thing in looking at these figures
is that an examination of them destroys this whole concept of trying to meet the problems of confederation by surrendering to the provinces their tax potential. Every once in a while when some matter arises where the federal government is seeking to help the provinces we have members rise and say that the solution lies in giving the provinces a larger share of the tax field. If they mean by that a larger adjustment of the equalization payments, this is true, but this is not usually what these people mean. What they mean is that the provinces should get more of the taxes which are collected within their borders.

We had a good example of this in the statement which was issued by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) on July 9 and which was reported in the Montreal Gazette. The report reads in part as follows:
Deputy Conservative leader Leon Balcer issued a policy statement yesterday-
The report goes on to say that he said that "the central government's refusal to restore to the provinces the sweeping tax and economic powers conscripted to meet war and economic crises" was responsible for the situation. The article continues:
He said that Quebec Conservatives rejected utterly Ottawa's contention that it was necessary for the central authority to retain and utilize these powers "to establish uniformity in the land through the application of national standards". The concept that the federal government, retaining these powers, could then help the provinces meet their constitutional obligations by "favours" and handouts was completely unacceptable in Quebec.
The article reports him further as follows:
He cited federal Bill No. C-108, for the extension of family allowances, and thus touched the provincial field of social welfare, as an example of the kind of federal legislation which "exasperates the autonomist province of Quebec."
He goes on to say:
Under the Canadian constitution, the domains of social security and education are assigned to the provinces and should normally be administered by the provinces. The (federal) government should return to the provinces a much larger field of taxation to give them the power to discharge conscientiously their responsibilities, such as those of social security and education.
May I ask-

If I may develop my argument, then my friend can ask me a question afterwards. If the hon. member for Three Rivers or anyone else who follows this argument, means the federal government should return to the provinces a much larger share of the aggregate pool of income, corporation and succession duties, then I agree with him. But this is not what the member said, and I take it it is not what he meant. He said that the federal government should return to the provinces a much larger field of taxation. I want to point out to those people who constantly take this position that if we take any one of the years in the table which I have just asked to be put on Hansard, we will find that if we had turned over to the provinces the entire field of taxation for income taxes, corporation taxes and succession duties, the province of Newfoundland would have obtained less money than it is getting now. In 1961-62 it would have obtained $5,600,000 20220-411
Federal-Provincial Relations less; 1960-61, $8,600,000 less; 1959-60, $12,100,000 less.
If Prince Edward Island had received the whole of the taxation revenues collected within its borders in 1961-62, it would have received $3 million less than it got in that year under these equalization payments. In 1960-61, it would have obtained $3,200,000 less; 1959-60, $3,700,000 less. The point I want to make is that when members, particularly members from the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, speak of allowing the provinces to meet their constitutional responsibilities by turning over to them a larger share of the tax field, they are losing sight of the fact that there are provinces in Canada where there is not the tax potential and that giving them a larger share of the tax field will not help them because the tax potential is not there.
It is for this reason I am heartily in support of the system of federal-provincial fiscal relations which we have. I criticize the formula. I think there are many things wrong with the formula. However, I do not believe we can build a country unless we think in terms of the fiscal needs of the provinces and not just the fiscal potential of the provinces, because there are provinces, particularly the Atlantic provinces, which cannot possibly meet their constitutional responsibilities even if the federal government withdrew entirely from the tax field and left them all the revenue that is collected in those provinces.
In other words, I think we must never lose sight of the basic principles that were laid down by the Rowell-Sirois commission, which pointed out that if we were going to have in Canada a great country, if we were going to have a certain minimum standard of health, welfare and education, if a Canadian citizen in one part of Canada was going to have equality of opportunity with another Canadian citizen in another part of Canada, then there must be some pooling and some sharing of the tax revenues, particularly the tax revenues which are jointly occupied by the federal and provincial governments, namely income, corporation and inheritance taxes.
May I ask a question?
Yes.
Can the hon. member explain these statistics to us because I must admit that I do not understand exactly what he means by these figures?

Well, I could do it more easily if my hon. friend would tell me what his difficulty is. Let me take 1961-62. If my

Federal-Provincial Relations friend looks at the total column he will see that the total amount collected for the three tax fields in Canada was $3,729,500,000; that was divided and the provinces got $976,600,000 and the federal government got $2,752,900,000. In other words, the federal government got 74 per cent of the total revenue collected in these fields and the provinces got 26 per cent.
Now, how was that 26 per cent divided amongst the provinces? Newfoundland got 118 per cent; in other words, they got 18 per cent more than was actually collected within their borders. Nova Scotia got 65 per cent of what was collected within its borders. Prince Edward Island got 159 per cent; in other words, it got 59 per cent more than was collected and it got it out of the general pool of tax revenues. New Brunswick got 82 per cent; Quebec, 28 per cent of the taxes collected in that province; Ontario got 18 per cent; Manitoba, 30 per cent; Saskatchewan, 56 per cent; Alberta, 30 per cent and British Columbia, 22 per cent.

Would the hon. member permit another question? How can he arrive at a total federal-provincial collection of $3,700 million when the federal government alone collected over $6 billion and the provincial governments collected as much as that? How can he arrive at a total of $3,700 million?
If the hon. member will look at the line at the top he will see that this is a distribution of personal income, corporation and estate taxes; just the three tax fields.
No sales tax?

No, we are talking about the three tax fields which are jointly occupied and which are the concern of this legislation because federal-provincial fiscal relations has to do only with the three shared tax fields.
How do you explain Newfoundland's federal share at minus $5 million? How can they collect a minus amount of tax revenue?
I have already explained that, but I will do it again.
We do not understand the language.

The total amount collected in Newfoundland in personal, corporation and estate taxes in the year 1961-62 was $31,800,000. Now, the province, under this equalization formula, got $37,400,000; in other words, they got $5,600,000 more than was collected in their province. This is why I keep arguing that to say, as some members did

when the school loans measure was before the house, we should give the provinces another one percentage point or two percentage points in income tax abatement, so far as Newfoundland or Prince Edward Island are concerned there is not much use giving them another 2 per cent of the income tax field, because they are already getting more than is being collected within their borders.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, the plea I am making is that those of us who live in provinces where our revenues per capita from these tax fields are above the national average and who sometimes argue that if we were to keep the taxes collected in our provinces we could discharge all our constitutional responsibilities and the federal government could get out of these fields entirely and concern itself with running the post office and the armed services, forget that there are provinces in Canada that would be bankrupt. There are provinces in Canada whose standards of education, health, welfare, roads and other services would be greatly reduced.
That is why I make this appeal to hon. members who live in the wealthier provinces, that these federal-provincial relations are part of an attempt to meet the goal which was set by the Rowell-Sirois commission, namely that as Canadians we accept our sense of responsibility for Canadians in other parts of Canada, particularly in those parts of Canada where people are less fortunate than people in other parts. If we are ever going to have a really great country it will only come about if we are willing to share some part of these tax revenues. That is what we are doing under these federal-provincial relations.
The taxes are going into a pool, as it were, and the provinces are getting back revenue under equalization payments roughly according to their needs. I should qualify that by saying I think we have departed a long way from the basis of fiscal need laid down by the Rowell-Sirois commission, but at least the minister is making some improvement under his most recent arrangements with the provinces. We have come from equalizing to the national average, up to equalizing to the top two provinces, and the minister has agreed to a further two percentage points in abatement of personal income taxes, and another 25 per cent abatement in estate taxes.
In this table which I asked to have printed in Hansard it shows that in 1961-62 26 per cent of this total from the three tax fields, went back to the provinces, and the changes

which the minister is now proposing will bring the provinces' share up to roughly 30 per cent. I wonder if the minister agrees with that. I am asking the minister whether these changes will mean that the provinces will get roughly about 30 per cent of the total revenues coming from these tax fields?

Mr. Speaker, I want to close by saying that we in this party are in full and complete agreement with the principle of equalization in federal-provincial relations, and we are fully in agreement with moving steadily toward a greater measure of fiscal equity as between the various provinces. We think the federal government has a responsibility to do this out of the taxes which are collected all over Canada on the wealth which is created all over Canada, and in many cases created in a different province from where it is taxed. We think these changes in the legislation will help to discharge the responsibility of assisting the provinces which are less fortunate and of equalizing the discrepancies which exist as between the different regions of Canada.
I hope that we will keep this principle of equalization. As a matter of fact we have been departing from it and I hope we will reverse the trend, and we are beginning to do it. For a while we moved a long way from the policy of fiscal need. We are now beginning to swing back to a greater recognition of the principle of fiscal need, and we are also going in the right direction in that we are increasing the share of the total revenues from the three tax fields which are to be made available to the provinces for the discharge of their responsibilities.
As I said a moment ago, in 1961-62 about 26 per cent of the total amount of taxes col-20220-411J
Federal-Provincial Relations lected in these fields went to the provinces, and I think that under the changes which are being proposed this will be brought close to 30 per cent. The responsibilities which the provinces have are growing in geometric progression, particularly in education but also in health and welfare, and I think the clay will come in Canada when 50 per cent of the gross revenues from these three fields will have to be allocated to the provinces on an equalization basis. And when that day comes I think the provinces will be much better able to discharge their responsibilities.
There can be no doubt that the provinces need more money. The way to give them more money is not to turn tax fields over to them, which would enable some provinces to meet their responsibilities but would leave other provinces worse off than they are now. The way to help the provinces discharge their responsibilities is to continue this pooling system, these equalization measures, and by giving the provinces a larger share with the eventual aim of seeing to it that about half the total revenues from the three tax fields in question find their way back to the provinces. If that were done the federal government could get rid of a lot of its conditional grants. These conditional grants in many cases are burdensome and difficult to administer and are not always equitable.
I hope the time comes when 40 per cent or 50 per cent of the revenues from these tax fields is returned to the provinces, and then the federal government, in return, could discontinue many of these conditional grants, and everyone would be happier because the federal government would be out of fields in which it has not any real constitutional responsibility while the provinces, on the other hand, would have by right under these federal-provincial arrangements the revenue to discharge the responsibilities which belong to them under our constitution.

Mr. Speaker, I did not take the opportunity to speak on this matter at resolution stage and there are a number of general remarks I wish to make at this time respecting the many amendments proposed to the federal-provincial fiscal arrangements.
When the Minister of Finance spoke on resolution stage, I believe it was on July 7, he said we should not be misled by the innocence of the resolution that had been on the order paper for a number of days, and certainly in so far as the impact of that innocent resolution is concerned he said a mouthful. We had not expected legislation that

Federal-Provincial Relations would involve so many and so profound changes which, by 1966-67, will amount to some $265 million annually.
Tonight I want to speak briefly about five different areas of financial arrangements between the provinces and the federal government, some of which are contained in the amendment, and some which should be but are not. First of all there is the matter of revenue received from the development of natural resources being included in the equalization formula. There is the matter of authorizing federal crown corporations to pay sales tax, not only from this date forward but to make a grant in lieu of sales tax as if it had been in effect from April, 1962. There is the matter of income tax incurred by privately owned utilities and there is also the matter of the cost-sharing arrangement between the federal government and the provinces respecting hospitalization.
At the outset, as one representing a constituency in Alberta, I think I am entitled to say that the province of Alberta-the government of Alberta-has always shown a high level of willingness to co-operate and be reasonable with the federal government in all the negotiations which have taken place on the subject of tax-sharing. If I may, I should like to quote some of the remarks which were made by the premier of Alberta prior to the federal-provincial conference held here in Ottawa on November 25, 1963, because it is important when discussing the discrimination which we feel is present in this bill to understand the concept which the government of Alberta has of federal-provincial fiscal arrangements.
First of all, the government of Alberta regards the following four points as being particularly important.
(1)	The necessity to evolve an arrangement under which each government will be assured sufficient financial resources to enable it to discharge its constitutional responsibilities without loss of its rightful sovereignty and without imposing oppressive burdens of taxation and debt upon its people.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam has just reviewed the problems which some of the provinces would experience in this respect if there were no such thing as equalization payments. I do not intend to repeat all that, but in essence, I agree, and I think it is evident from this statement by the premier of Alberta that he, too, agrees with this concept. To continue:
(2)	The provision of effective incentives to stimulate more active economic growth and the forms such incentives should take and the means by which they can best be provided.

I think we must come to the realization, sooner or later-and the sooner the better, in my opinion-that if we are to stimulate a more active rate of economic growth we must keep uppermost in our minds at least some of the time the likely effect of additional taxation on private industry and private enterprises throughout Canada which, after all, are the foundation upon which all this taxation rests.
The premier of Alberta went on to mention the importance of the following:
(3)	Shared-cost programs and the desirability of devising more acceptable methods of providing federal fiscal aid to legitimate projects which by their nature are of national as well as provincial importance and concern.
I think that is self-explanatory. The fourth point he made prior to this federal-provincial conference was this:
(4)	Practical monetary and fiscal programs which may be undertaken to assist in resolving the financial problems confronting governments, industry and the Canadian people generally, with a view to ensuring a supply of private and public capital adequate to finance economic expansion and social capital projects and maintain effective consumer demand without further pyramiding the public and private debt.
This is something of which we must ever be mindful when we talk about more and more social services and quick progress in this direction, namely that there is a level, or a limit-a point of diminishing returns as far as the welfare of the Canadian people is concerned. The premier went on to say:
While these and other related matters properly are included on the agenda and should be fully and frankly discussed, it is the view of the government of Alberta that the initial objective of this conference should be to clarify the respective responsibilities of the two levels of government and adopt a set of sound principles or ground rules on the basis of which, we believe, practical procedures can be developed for the solution of the financial and economic and social problems we face. Unless this is done as an initial step, the conference discussions will, in our opinion, be inconclusive and the problems which have brought us together will remain largely unsolved.
It has long been the contention of the government of Alberta that the pie is only so large, no matter how we cut it. If all levels of government, and all the provinces, are continually to make financial demands having in mind what they think are their obligations, we must do one of two things-either increase the size of the pie, or adjust our demands so as to fit it. This is not easy. It takes a government with a great deal of courage to say to the people of Canada, or to the people it represents, that immediately, in this very year, the total amount of the services they

demand from their government will have to be paid for. This is a situation to which we will come, eventually. We have reached a position in Canada today where $1,035 million out of rather more than $6 billions, or around 15 per cent of the total revenue from all sources, is going to pay interest on the national debt. We are anticipating another deficit of $455 million plus the supplementary estimates, so we shall be faced with even higher interest payments next year. Some year, some time, whether it is in 1964, 1967 or 1970, we must have the courage to say to the Canadian people: That which you demand must be paid for, and paid for this year.
I need go back only to 1935 to illustrate the situation I have in mind. In 1935, when the Social Credit government was first elected in the province of Alberta, there was a desperate situation with respect to debt and debt service charges. Many people do not understand this. In that year, out of a total budget for all purposes amounting to something over $15 million, $8 million was allocated to the payment of interest on the provincial debt. More than 50 per cent of all the revenue going to the province from all sources was being paid over in interest charges. Surely we do not have to wait until a situation like that occurs before taking steps to deal with it. Surely we do not have to keep rolling from one temporary expedient to another until we reach a situation so desperate that we find the courage to say to the people we represent: Let us slow down and sober up a bit with regard to these expenditures, and see what we can do. The premier of Alberta has pleaded at one after another of the federal-provincial conferences that there should be a realistic and sober analysis made. So far we continue to go on as if something magic is going to come along and straighten out this financial mess for us.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, there are four or five other matters that I want to deal with in connection with this bill. The first one is extremely important and we have not as yet been able to get a satisfactory answer from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon). It is as to why he has included revenue from natural resources in calculating the amount of tax equalization? The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) asked him these questions: Why not sales tax? Why not other forms of taxation?

Liquor revenue.
Federal-Provincial Relations

Yes, liquor revenue, and all the other provincial taxes and sources of revenue. Why are they left out and natural resource revenue taken in? Is this some form of taxation, or another way of obtaining revenue in lieu of taxation-although in many respects I do not think it is taxation at all? Why include it?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder if the hon. member would allow me to ask him a question? Is it not true that in the province from which the hon. member comes, in their own published accounts they show these revenues from natural resources as tax revenues? That is the way they record them in their own accounts, in their published statements. Is that not a fact?

No, Mr. Speaker, that is not a fact at all. Certainly they include it as public revenue, but they do not include it as taxation. I would point out to the Minister of Finance that if he goes into any other province the liquor tax, the retail sales tax, the licence taxes, gasoline tax and all the other taxes are included in the records as provincial revenue in just the same way as the three taxes that are used as a basis, or are supposed to be used as a basis, in this regard. If the minister is saying the reason is that the province does their accounting on this basis, he will also have to agree, if he is to follow that argument through to its logical conclusion, that they include all these other forms of taxation as well.
But that is not all, Mr. Speaker. In addition, there is no provision in the bill, as far as I can see, for the cost of maintaining this revenue from natural resources. In the province of British Columbia, for example, great amounts of money are spent in the protection of forests and the development of the continuity of forests and all that involves. But instead of using the net amount that comes from this kind of natural resource revenue, they use the gross. In those provinces where they do not have a high gross natural resource revenue, they also do not have any expense in order to maintain that resource. In the province of Alberta the gross amount received from oil and gas happens to be the highest source of revenue, but there are such things as forest products, coal and a number of other things. In the case of oil and gas, for example, there is also a large expenditure which is required to supervise the operation of this whole business in that province. The Alberta oil and gas conservation board is only one example; in addition they have to set up

Federal-Provincial Relations a large administrative staff to see that this industry does in fact operate so they have the optimum production from the gas and oil fields which they find. Surely this expense, if you want to be a little fair, ought to be deducted before any amount is posted in this formula for equalization.
We cannot understand the reason for this. One or two suggestions have been made. It has been suggested that perhaps somebody in the Department of Finance, somebody in the government, for reasons which have not as yet been explained, arrived at some kind of distribution of federal tax moneys and then concocted a formula to meet that pre-determined amount. That is what we believe; there does not seem to be any other explanation for it. We cannot understand how else the Minister of Finance could have arrived at such a figure.
I look at the table he presented to the House of Commons on July 7, indicating the amounts that will be payable, under the changes in the equalization formula, for the year 196465. I am not going to read this all back into Hansard, but it is to be found at page 5184. We find there are certain payments to Newfoundland, Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and all the other provinces except Alberta and British Columbia. For Alberta there is nothing; for British Columbia there is nothing. For the fiscal year 1965-66 we find the very same thing. They are going to change the formula again to 19-9-50, but for Alberta and British Columbia, nothing. For 1966-67, under the changes in the equalization formula to 20-9-50, the province of Alberta will get nothing; the province of British Columbia, nothing. The province of Saskatchewan will get a wee bit-it is not quite nil, but it is very low-under these changes.
But this is simply not fair; it is not fair to count the gross amount as revenue, because it certainly is not net revenue such as the collection of personal income taxes, corporation taxes and succession duties. The amounts collected under all those three forms of taxation are net, but what is collected from the sale of natural resources, and from royalties, and so on, is not net. Then there is the other point made by the hon. member for Jasper-Edson (Mr. Horner) which must be considered. Some of this revenue that is collected from natural resources is not in fact what you might call income at all because it is derived from the sale of capital assets in some respects. For example there are sales of crown reservations. While the province does not surrender the ownership of these crown


reservations-they lease them-nevertheless they lease for a long period of time the right to develop. This is not, in the ordinary sense, income from natural resources. There has been no explanation as to why this was included, and we think it is discrimination against the province of Alberta particularly, and to a lesser extent but to far too great an extent, if I may put it that way, against the province of British Columbia.
We are wondering why this was done. Have we reached the stage in federal-provincial fiscal relations where it is necessary to talk tough, to talk about separation and make all kinds of other threats before the government of the day understands the language you are trying to speak? I hope not, Mr. Speaker. But in view of the conditions that are going to exist in federal-provincial fiscal relations after this bill comes into effect, it appears this is the only conclusion one can come to. As I said, the province of Alberta has over the years-and I do not think any responsible minister will deny this-gone out of its way to be reasonable and fair.
I have been at Social Credit conventions when this matter has been brought up and I have heard the provincial treasurer and premier of Alberta say that when you are asking for something from some other level of government the fair thing to do is to put yourself in their position and ask them for what you would be willing to give. Another matter concerns shared hospitalization costs. I could cite many quotations to the house where the Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister, and so on, have said that every province in the country should have the right to run its own affairs the way it wants; that all people across Canada should be treated in the same way. The province of Alberta does not levy a hospitalization premium. It does not collect by means of a sales tax some of the revenue which it needs. Rather it chooses to pay some of the cost of operating its hospitals by means of what it calls deterrent fees or co-insurance fees. I have asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) about this matter a number of times. I have asked her why it is that the federal government subtracts $1.50 or $2 a day from the cost of operating the hospitals before the federal and provincial governments share the balance, but she has evaded the question. The last time I asked her she said that it was a matter for the Minister of Finance, who deals with fiscal relationships with the provinces. We would like an explanation from the Minister of Finance as to why

regulations have been instituted which are a direct interference with the way in which the province of Alberta happens to choose to run its hospitalization program.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. member would permit a question. Would he not consider that a charge which is made to a patient at the time the patient is admitted to hospital in order to meet an uninsured portion of that patient's bill is therefore not liable to the theory of the hospitalization insurance act with regard to cost sharing?

I am not sure I understand the import of the hon. member's question, but the fact is that some provinces have levied a retail sales tax and have claimed that this was for hospitalization purposes only. Other provinces collect a premium from the residents and say that this is to be part of the cost of the province's share of operating the hospitalization program. The province of Alberta happens to be of the opinion that a small deterrent fee, co-insurance fee, call it what you will, is a proper and beneficial way of collecting part of the provincial share of their hospitalization program.
We do not think that it is any of the federal government's business how the province of Alberta collects the revenues which it assigns to certain of its social programs, including hospitalization. It is not a large item; this is costing the residents of Alberta about $2 million a year. It is also not a burden. Many of the hospital wards in the province of Alberta cost as much as $24 a day per bed to operate and the fee levied on the patient during the days when he occupies a bed is from $1.60 to $2 per day. Therefore this amount is substantially less than 10 per cent of the actual cost. What is more, if anyone requires hospitalization and is unable to pay the $2 a day, the provincial government will pay that as well. When it comes to sharing the costs, the federal government claims that it is paying 50 per cent of the cost of hospitalization across the country, but in the province of Alberta, because of the regulations which have been imposed regarding this matter and because of other unapproved costs, the share of the federal government amounts to 39.11 per cent, I believe it is. Therefore, we think this is an interference in provincial rights and is a discrimination against the province of Alberta. What is more, we are of the opinion that this would not be tolerated by some of the other provinces in the country. If the only kind of language which is understood by the federal govern-
Federal-Provincial Relations ment is getting tough and being unco-operative, then we may have to change to that kind of language.
There is also the question of sales tax. Why is the federal government now authorizing the federal crown corporations to pay provincial sales tax? This is indirectly further distribution of federal money through crown corporations which are subsidized. It cannot be anything else. The province of Alberta does not levy a retail sales tax, and the other retail sales taxes across the country are at varying levels. This will be a bonus to those provinces which levy the highest tax. We cannot understand why this particular tax was selected to redistribute federal money to the provinces.
On May 13 I asked a question of the former parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Finance, now minister of revenue (Mr. Benson), when the bill to authorize crown corporations to pay these taxes was passed. It is reported on page 3239 of Hansard as follows:
Has any consideration been given to making cash payments to those provinces which do not levy sales tax, in lieu of tax revenue from these corporations?
The parliamentary secretary replied:
No consideration has been given to this matter. It would be extremely difficult to calculate how much revenue would have been realized had a sales tax been imposed, or at what rate it might have been imposed.
After that answer from the former parliamentary secretary, the government are now making under this bill the payment of sales tax retroactive to April 1962. If it is so difficult to calculate how much the grant would be to provinces which do not levy a sales tax, how is the government going to calculate how much the tax will be for these past two years? This is a complete somersault and is a change which is too serious to be taken lightly. The Minister of Finance has said that we should treat all people and all provinces alike. Why is no consideration being given to distributing some money under some other form of taxation? It is not too difficult to find out what the figure will be for provinces who opt out of the students loans legislation, and in all other types of programs in which certain provinces do not wish to participate the government are able to calculate the amount of the grant due in lieu of participation. But in this case we are told the amount is too difficult to calculate. What is more, there has been no consideration of this matter. A year or two ago the province of British Columbia, after having re-

One of these principles has been mentioned already this evening by two of the previous speakers. There has to be, as was suggested previously and again tonight, some consideration given to the question of the nature of this income, for obviously part of the income from the natural resources of a province is drawn from

Federal-Provincial Relations non-renewable resources, from minerals, oil and natural gas. The income is being derived from a wasting resource. There is nothing the province or anyone can do to renew that resource. Once it is gone, it is gone forever. Once it has been used, there will be no further income from it; there will be no renewal of income from that particular resource-it has been expended.
Therefore to take into account revenue as a consequence of a sale of that resource as part of the income of a province is undoubtedly dangerous. Serious consideration should be given by the federal government to some formula by which a province is credited with the depletion of its resources. Unless such a depletion allowance is provided in the consideration of income of the province, this formula is not fair and is not equitable. There are other resources, forest resources and water resources, that can be used, renewed and used again. There, again, it is not equitable that the province should be charged with all the income derived from those resources in considering its share of tax equalization payments, because obviously these renewable resources must be managed.
Each province must spend a substantial amount of money annually in renewing its forest resources, protecting and to a substantial extent renewing and perpetuating, through some measures that can be taken in some provinces, its water resources. These are charges upon the province which do not appear in the equation as indicated in this bill. If there is to be equity in the consideration of the economic wealth of the provinces, these factors must be taken into account by the federal government. There must be this recognition of depreciation of non-renewable resources, and recognition of the cost of perpetuating and preserving renewable resources.
I trust that the minister, when he comes to answer the comments made, will have some understanding of what I have just said, as I notice he is paying not the slightest attention. These factors have not been taken into account in any statement made by the government. The minister has not even caught up with my latest intervention, but I hope he will later.
I submit these factors must be taken into account if there is to be an equitable sharing of financial resources in the provinces. If the provinces are to have the responsibility for and the cost of administering, protecting and preserving their resources, the federal government in taking revenue from them and the provinces being required, in effect,
[Mr. Fleming (Okanagan-Revelstoke).l
to share that revenue with the federal government, the costs to the provinces must be taken into account by the federal government before it makes its assessment. I think that is fundamental and applies to any business. You simply do not milk your assets till they are gone and there is no asset left with which to produce future revenue. Any business can be destroyed pretty fast by not taking into account depreciation of assets. In the income tax and corporation tax structure of the federal government depreciation must be taken into account, and it must be taken into account in this formula which has been established by the federal government in arriving at which of the provinces shall not participate in equalization payments. The formula must also take into account that this will work to the benefit of some provinces which now benefit substantially from equalization payments and at the same time are provinces which can derive substantial revenue from the sale of natural resources. Such provinces might benefit from this consideration as well as provinces like British Columbia and Alberta, which find that their natural resource income deprives them of the right of participation in equalization payments under the present formula.
Another matter which has been mentioned many times in the house, both in the course of the resolution debate and also this evening, so therefore I will not labour the point, is that an equally important point with regard to this federal-provincial fiscal revision act does not appear in the bill. It is something which is absent from this bill but has not been absent from the considerations of this house during the past few days. It is an indication of government policy on sharing the cost of highway building in the provinces.
Late in July the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) indicated that this fall there is to be a dominion-provincial conference on national highways policy. Naturally no one would argue with the necessity for such a conference; members from every province would welcome one. But it was assumed that at that time there would be a general assessment of the federal role in highway construction in the provinces, whether the federal government had in fact any role or responsibility at all. It could be assumed that when this announcement was made about this conference, federal government participation in road building programs in the provinces on a major scale would wait until after the conference. That might be one

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
reason why this particular aspect of federal-provincial co-operation is not included in this bill.
Within the past 48 hours-in fact yesterday-we found that although there is to be a highways conference in the fall the government has come to an ad hoc arrangement with one of the provinces and decided to spend $13 million on a purely provincial road. It is not even a road which could be considered in the national context. It might have come within the general context of roads to resources or even forest access roads, but we know that the present administration has eliminated both those programs and they are gone. Therefore we cannot find any over-all national policy to account for this sudden, one-shot roadbuilding program introduced in one province.
I am not arguing against the merits of such a program but I am arguing against this ad hoc arrangement, this one-shot deal undertaken in the face of what we had assumed would be federal government policy to consult with all the provinces to arrive at a national highways policy. Then when one is confronted with this bill and finds that it provides that a province like British Columbia is not to participate to any extent in tax equalization programs, and when one finds that the roads to resources and forest access programs have been discontinued and no other provision made for a joint federal-provincial roadbuilding program, which is of tremendous importance, if not of vital necessity, to the provinces, it is clear this bill has been circumvented in this sudden, one-shot, ad hoc arrangement with one of the provinces. This is in defiance of the very principles established in the bill and contained in other government statements, including that of the Minister of Public Works, relating to a national highways program.
In view of the fact that there seems to be plenty of precedent in the house tonight for a member speaking on behalf of his own province and perhaps considering provincial interests over national interests, I must say that it seems to me that this is something which is being thrust upon us by the provisions of this bill and the announcement made yesterday, coupled with the inadequacy of federal policy in regard to British Columbia, the particular problems of communications in that province and the absolute necessity for federal interest in highways policy as it applies to the west coast in particular. In this regard I refer to the necessity for linking the Pacific coast of Canada more satisfactorily with the rest of Canada through direct highway access to the seaports on the coast.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it 10.30.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I presume that we are continuing with this debate tomorrow.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext: Tomorrow we will continue with this debate and the committee stage. Should it be concluded tomorrow, and I have every reason to believe it will be concluded early tomorrow, we will take up main estimates, those of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration and the Department of Labour. Then on Monday we will go on with the flag debate. Should this debate not conclude tomorrow it will be the first item of business on Monday, followed by the debate on the flag resolution.
A motion to adjourn the house under provisional standing order 39A deemed to have been moved:

Mr. Speaker, the question I posed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) yesterday and which he refused to answer was based on an independent survey carried out by Gruneau Research Limited, an international and highly respected research organization, in which two questions were asked of those interviewed; whether they preferred the retention of the red ensign as Canada's national flag, or the design favoured by the Prime Minister and proposed by the government. The results of the survey indicate majority support for the retention of the red ensign in every province of Canada with the exception of Quebec.
Surely in view of this new evidence and the show of strength across this nation in favour of the Canadian red ensign, no responsible Prime Minister would desire to move forward with a flag design which he learns is acceptable by the majority in only one province of this nation. Surely the evidence tendered is of such importance from the point of view of national unity that a responsible government can reach only one of two conclusions; either to withdraw the design proposed, or to support the initiation of a national plebiscite which would give Canadians a number of preferences from which to select the
6516	HOUSE OF
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion flag of their choice. Surely this evidence produces the danger signals that tell the government to go slow on an issue which is of such an emotional nature that the very foundation on which confederation was built could erode to the point where we could well have difficulty in arriving at our 100th birthday. Surely the fact that there is overwhelming support in the province of Quebec and only minority support in the remaining nine provinces should not be a reason for his adamant stand to push forward with his resolution.
I am not so naive, Mr. Speaker, as to think the Prime Minister was not aware of the results of the survey in question. One must then ask the question as to why he has refused to answer my question and, indeed, alter the stubborn and irresponsible stand he now takes. There has never been an issue before this parliament where more backroom, clandestine, political intrigues have been worked out between the government and the splinter parties. No better piece of evidence is available than the statement yesterday by the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) which appears on page 6439 of Hansard:
I believe the government is unanimous with us to vote against part B and in favour of part A.
How much longer does the Prime Minister consider he can carry on in this dictatorial manner of pressing forward with a flag design that is acceptable in one province and unacceptable to a majority in the remaining nine provinces, or is this only the first phase of a grand plan to make Canada a republic? Lest you think I am exaggerating, let me quote directly from Hansard. Here is what one member said who is supporting the Prime Minister's flag. I refer to page 4946 of Hansard.

We are proud to endorse the resolution concerning a distinctive flag, but we are determined to get rid of the union jack. We want "O Canada" as our anthem but we are unwilling to recognize "God Save the Queen".
Another said, as found on page 4964:
I have advocated for 25 years the establishment of a Canadian republic and called for the red ensign and union jack to be set aside.

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio; Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when this question was asked on August 5 the Speaker said, as found on page 6421 of Hansard:
Order. In my opinion this question might properly be asked at the time the flag debate commences.
In view of that ruling, Mr. Speaker, 1 think it is not altogether correct to say that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) refused to answer the question. He was prevented from answering the question by the Speaker ruling the question out of order.
I might also refer to the answer that the Prime Minister made at that time to the question put to him by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer). The Prime Minister said:
When the debate on this issue is resumed, which I hope will be very shortly, all these matters may be considered.
There is every indication that the debate on the flag resolution will be resumed on Monday or at the very latest on Tuesday, and I think that is the proper time to reply to all these questions posed by the hon. member for Cumberland.

speechtext:
The proper time, but will answers be given?
